title: All Bell Inequalities With A Quantum Advantage In The Minimal Scenario Are Self-testing
authors: Mu-En Liu, Andrea Zingarofalo, Victor Barizien, Jean-Daniel Bancal
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the minimal Bell scenario, all extremal quantum correlations are known, but the Tsirelson inequalities that delimit the quantum set remain poorly understood. We study which correlations can maximize a given Tsirelson inequality, and conversely, which inequalities are maximized by a given correlation. We show that every Tsirelson inequality with quantum advantage is maximized by a single, extremal correlation, and thus self-tests the corresponding realization. This characterizes all self-tests based on linear Bell inequalities in this scenario. We also show that at most a two-dimensional family of inequalities can be maximized by a nonlocal extremal correlation. We identify these as polygons for a family of correlations realized by qubit states of arbitrary entanglement. This allows us to deduce that the quantum set is not self-dual.
tldr: The paper proves that every Bell inequality with a quantum advantage in the minimal scenario is maximized by a unique extremal quantum correlation and therefore provides a self-test.
motivation: Tsirelson inequalities in the minimal Bell scenario are poorly understood despite complete knowledge of extremal quantum correlations, and a characterization of linear-inequality-based self-tests was missing.
method: The authors analyze the relation between Tsirelson inequalities and extremal quantum correlations, characterizing which correlations maximize given inequalities and which inequalities are maximized by nonlocal extremal correlations.
result: They show that all advantageous Tsirelson inequalities self-test a single extremal correlation, that at most a two-dimensional family of inequalities can be maximized by a nonlocal extremal correlation, and that the quantum set is not self-dual.
conclusion: This fully characterizes self-tests from linear Bell inequalities in the minimal scenario and establishes structural properties of the quantum correlation set.

While all extremal quantum correlations in this scenario are known, the inequalities that delimit the quantum set have remained poorly understood. The authors address two complementary questions: which correlations can maximize a given Tsirelson inequality, and conversely, which inequalities are maximized by a given correlation. They prove that every Tsirelson inequality with quantum advantage is maximized by a single extremal correlation, which implies that the inequality self-tests the corresponding quantum realization. This provides a complete characterization of all self-tests based on linear Bell inequalities in the minimal scenario. Furthermore, they show that at most a two-dimensional family of inequalities can be maximized by a nonlocal extremal correlation. They identify these as polygons for a family of correlations realized by qubit states with arbitrary entanglement. As a consequence, they deduce that the quantum set is not self-dual, meaning that the set of quantum correlations is not equal to its dual under the standard inner product. The work combines geometric methods with quantum information concepts to yield new insights into the geometry of quantum correlations.

title: Fidelity Determines The Minimum Error Of Quantum Recovery
authors: Dario Picozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Even a recovery that maximizes worst-input entanglement fidelity can retain avoidable errors in subsequent measurements. Entanglement fidelity is the probability of passing a test of whether the state and its entanglement were preserved; infidelity is the probability of failing it. Operational error is the largest possible change in any measurement probability, quantified by the normalized diamond distance. For every finite-dimensional noise channel and fixed encoding, we prove that operational error and worst-input entanglement infidelity have the same minimum over all recovery operations. The proof constructs one final unitary (a reversible quantum operation) that makes any recovery's operational error no greater than its original worst-input entanglement infidelity. With a retained noise record, we determine the optimal error and characterize all optimal decoders subject to a Kraus-rank limit for each outcome. For a fixed decoded channel, a semidefinite program finds the optimal final unitary in the low-error regime. We characterize all optimal final corrections and show that, at a fixed error floor [MATH], the operational optimizers' sensitivity to residual unitary errors of size [MATH] is at worst of order [MATH], while the canonical polar correction has quadratic sensitivity.
tldr: The paper proves that for any finite-dimensional noise channel and fixed encoding, the minimum operational error over recovery operations equals the minimum worst-input entanglement infidelity.
motivation: Recovery operations optimized for entanglement fidelity may still leave avoidable operational errors in later measurements, so a sharper connection is needed between entanglement fidelity and measurement-level error.
method: The author constructs a final unitary correction showing any recovery's operational error, measured by normalized diamond distance, can be bounded by its worst-input entanglement infidelity, and uses semidefinite programming to characterize optimal final corrections under low error.
result: The minima of operational error and worst-input entanglement infidelity over all recoveries coincide, optimal decoders are characterized under a Kraus-rank constraint, and optimal operational corrections are shown to be more robust to residual unitary errors than the canonical polar correction.
conclusion: Entanglement infidelity determines the fundamental operational recovery error, and appropriately chosen final unitaries can achieve optimal robustness against residual errors.

The authors prove that for any finite-dimensional noise channel and fixed encoding, the minimum operational error over all recovery operations equals the minimum worst-input entanglement infidelity. The proof is constructive: given any recovery, they build a final unitary (a reversible quantum operation) that ensures the operational error of the modified recovery is no greater than the original worst-input entanglement infidelity. This shows that optimizing entanglement fidelity does not inherently leave avoidable operational errors in subsequent measurements, contrary to what the title suggests might be a concern. The result holds for all finite dimensions and any noise channel, without assumptions on the recovery's form.

The paper then extends the analysis to scenarios with a retained noise record (e.g., when the environment is monitored). They determine the optimal error and characterize all optimal decoders subject to a Kraus-rank limit for each outcome. For a fixed decoded channel, they formulate a semidefinite program (SDP) to find the optimal final unitary in the low-error regime. Specifically, they show that at a fixed error floor 0<ε<1, the operational optimizers' sensitivity to residual unitary errors of size s is at worst of order s^{4/3}, whereas the canonical polar correction has quadratic sensitivity (order s^2). This indicates that operational optimizers can be more robust to certain small errors than the polar correction, which is commonly used.

The sensitivity analysis reveals a trade-off: while polar correction is optimal for entanglement fidelity, it may not be optimal for operational error in the presence of residual errors, and the proposed optimizers achieve better worst-case sensitivity.

title: Separability And Lower Bounds Of Concurrence Via Symmetric Measurement Correlations
authors: Yuhang Xie, Yanjun Chu, Shao-Ming Fei
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement is a central issue in quantum information science, particularly for unknown quantum states. Based on symmetric measurement correlation matrices, we present a family of separability criteria that can be experimentally applied without state tomography, and recover some related existing criteria as special cases. Using the constructed correlation matrices, we further derive a class of lower bounds of concurrence. Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate that our criteria outperform some existing separability criteria in entanglement detection, and that the obtained lower bounds on concurrence are tighter than known counterparts.
tldr: The paper introduces separability criteria and concurrence lower bounds based on symmetric measurement correlation matrices that can be applied experimentally without full state tomography.
motivation: Entanglement detection and quantification for unknown quantum states is a central challenge in quantum information, and tomography-free methods are particularly valuable experimentally.
method: The authors construct families of symmetric measurement correlation matrices and use them to derive separability criteria and lower bounds on concurrence, recovering existing criteria as special cases.
result: Illustrative examples show that the new criteria outperform some existing separability tests and that the concurrence lower bounds are tighter than known counterparts.
conclusion: Symmetric measurement correlations provide a practical and effective framework for entanglement detection and quantification without state tomography.

title: Nonlocal Magic Of Fermions Is Bounded By Entanglement Fluctuations And Is Logarithmic For Free Fermions
authors: Raghav G. Jha, Dengyao Luo, Alexander F. Kemper, Bojko N. Bakalov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Free-fermion states are classically simulable, yet, written as qubits, they typically carry extensive magic, the quantum resource that stabilizer circuits lack. Part of this magic is nonlocal: local unitaries acting separately on two parts of the system cannot remove it. If these local unitaries are restricted to Gaussian ones, the nonlocal magic grows linearly with the number [MATH] of partially entangled fermion pairs. We show that this growth is an artifact of the Gaussian restriction: local Gaussian unitaries minimize the nonlocal stabilizer R\'enyi entropy for up to three pairs, but not from four pairs on. General local non-Gaussian unitaries that respect fermion parity take [MATH] free-fermion pairs to fermionic Bell pairs with a fidelity that decays at most as [MATH] compared to exponential decay with Gaussian unitaries, so the nonlocal magic drops from linear to logarithmic in [MATH]. The reason is statistical --- Bell pairs have equal Schmidt weights, that is, a fully degenerate entanglement spectrum, and a state can stay far from them only if its Schmidt weights are spread over many orders of magnitude. This spread is measured by the capacity of entanglement [MATH], the variance of the entanglement Hamiltonian, and the nonlocal magic of any fermionic state grows at most logarithmically with [MATH]. Free-fermion pairs add to [MATH] independently, so [MATH] grows only linearly in [MATH], and this leads to the stabilizer fidelity decreasing at most as [MATH]. Almost all the magic of free fermions, including Hartree--Fock and BCS mean-field states, is therefore local.
tldr: The paper shows that the nonlocal magic of fermionic states is bounded by entanglement fluctuations, measured by the capacity of entanglement, and drops from linear to logarithmic growth under general parity-preserving local unitaries.
motivation: Free-fermion states are classically simulable but carry extensive magic when represented as qubits; the nonlocal part of this magic appeared to grow linearly under local Gaussian unitaries, prompting the question of whether this is a fundamental or Gaussian-restriction artifact.
method: The authors compare local Gaussian and general non-Gaussian fermion-parity-preserving unitaries using stabilizer Rényi entropy, and bound the distance to fermionic Bell pairs via the spread of Schmidt weights quantified by the capacity of entanglement.
result: General local non-Gaussian unitaries reduce free-fermion pairs to fermionic Bell pairs with fidelity decaying at most polynomially rather than exponentially, making nonlocal magic grow only logarithmically; the capacity of entanglement grows linearly, bounding nonlocal magic logarithmically.
conclusion: Almost all magic in free-fermion states, including Hartree-Fock and BCS mean-field states, is local; the nonlocal magic is fundamentally limited by entanglement fluctuations.

The authors focus on the nonlocal magic that cannot be removed by local unitaries acting on two parts of the system. Previous work showed that if local unitaries are restricted to Gaussian operations, the nonlocal magic grows linearly with the number m of partially entangled fermion pairs. This paper demonstrates that this linear growth is an artifact of the Gaussian restriction: local Gaussian unitaries minimize the nonlocal stabilizer Rényi entropy only for up to three pairs, but fail for four or more. By allowing general local non-Gaussian unitaries that respect fermion parity, the authors show that m free-fermion pairs can be transformed to fermionic Bell pairs with fidelity decaying at most as 1/√m, compared to exponential decay with Gaussian unitaries. Consequently, the nonlocal magic drops from linear to logarithmic in m. The underlying reason is statistical: Bell pairs have a fully degenerate entanglement spectrum (equal Schmidt weights), and a state can remain far from them only if its Schmidt weights are spread over many orders of magnitude. This spread is quantified by the capacity of entanglement C_E, the variance of the entanglement Hamiltonian. The authors prove that the nonlocal magic of any fermionic state grows at most logarithmically with C_E. Since free-fermion pairs add to C_E independently, C_E grows only linearly in m, leading to the stabilizer fidelity decreasing at most as 1/√m. Thus, almost all magic of free fermions, including Hartree-Fock and BCS mean-field states, is local.

title: Thermally-driven Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Daniel Valente Thiago Werlang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heat generation limits computation, classical and quantum, from single logic gates to entire data centers. However, an in principle limiting physical factor can sometimes be turned into a resource. In reservoir computing, energy dissipation is what gives a reservoir its fading memory. Here, we introduce a paradigm where the data injection itself is encoded on the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath. We derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout, and prove a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off which turns out to be a structural necessity, rather than a tunable dynamical regime, since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. We illustrate both results with a driven qubit, using a single free parameter, and with a pair of coupled qubits, where the breaking of a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable alone recovers just over half of it. This refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power. Our results relocate the memory-nonlinearity trade-off from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering (instead of Hamiltonian control) as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.
tldr: The paper introduces thermally driven quantum reservoir computing, where data are encoded in the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath and a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off is derived.
motivation: Heat generation is usually a limiting factor in computation, but in reservoir computing dissipation enables fading memory; the authors aim to turn this thermodynamic constraint into a resource by injecting data through bath temperature.
method: They derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout and prove a memory-nonlinearity trade-off, illustrating the results with a driven qubit and a pair of coupled qubits.
result: The trade-off is structural because the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration; in the coupled-qubit case, breaking a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space, but a single observable recovers just over half of it.
conclusion: The memory-nonlinearity trade-off is relocated from reservoir dynamics to the measurement channel, making observable choice and bath engineering the key physical levers for a thermally native quantum reservoir computer.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a paradigm for quantum reservoir computing where the input data is encoded in the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath, rather than in Hamiltonian parameters or coherent drives. The authors derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout observable to such thermal encoding, showing that the response is a sum over multi-time correlation functions of the reservoir's equilibrium state. They then prove a rigorous trade-off between memory (fading memory of past inputs) and nonlinearity (ability to compute nonlinear functions): increasing the coupling strength that injects data also increases the equilibration rate, which erases memory. This trade-off is structural, not a tunable dynamical regime, because the same coupling governs both data injection and thermalization. The results are illustrated with two examples: a driven qubit with a single free parameter, and a pair of coupled qubits where breaking a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable recovers just over half of it. The authors argue that this refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power, and that the memory-nonlinearity trade-off is relocated from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

They model the reservoir as a quantum system coupled to a thermal bath whose temperature is modulated in time to encode input data. Using the Kubo formula and perturbation theory in the system-bath coupling, they derive an exact expression for the readout's response as a sum over multi-time correlation functions of the reservoir's equilibrium state. This allows them to quantify memory (via the decay of correlation functions) and nonlinearity (via higher-order terms) and to prove a trade-off relation. The proof relies on the fact that the same coupling strength controls both the injection of data (the perturbation) and the equilibration rate (the decay of correlations), leading to a structural constraint. The authors then apply this framework to two concrete models: a driven qubit and a pair of coupled qubits. For the coupled qubits, they analyze the symmetry breaking and the dimensionality of the observable space, showing that a single observable can access only a fraction of the full space. The methodology is primarily theoretical, with numerical illustrations for the qubit examples.

title: Unifying First-Order Coherence, Concurrence, And Bell Correlations In Three-Flavor Neutrino Oscillations
authors: Bingbing Li, Tao Wu, Jiadong Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutrino oscillations provide a natural setting for investigating the quantum character of flavor conversion and the distribution of quantum resources over macroscopic distances. Here, we study exact relations among purity-based first-order coherence, pairwise concurrence, and the maximal Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) value in coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations. By expressing the evolving neutrino as a three-qubit single-excitation state, we derive the generally mixed two-qubit reductions and show that the squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode and its two associated squared concurrences sum to unity. Furthermore, a closed two-branch relation is obtained, showing that the maximal CHSH value of any reduced pair is determined by its average first-order coherence and concurrence. The branch structure follows from the correlation-tensor spectrum and yields exact conditions for CHSH violation. For the vacuum parameters and propagation ranges considered, electron preparation gives weak CHSH violations in electroncontaining pairs, while muon preparation produces a dominant utau pair with substantially stronger concurrence and Bell correlations. The comparison also identifies the thirdflavor contribution responsible for the different locations of concurrence and CHSH maxima. These results clarify the distribution of quantum correlations during flavor evolution and provide a basis for extensions to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.

result: The squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode plus its two associated squared concurrences sum to unity, and a closed two-branch formula determines the maximal CHSH value from average coherence and concurrence, yielding exact CHSH-violation conditions.
conclusion: These results clarify how quantum resources are distributed among neutrino flavors and provide a basis for extending the analysis to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.

title: Operational Characterizations And Resource Structure Of The Interactive Weight Of Quantum Instruments
authors: Yongxi He, Xin Hong, Yu Luo, Xiangzhen Zhou, Shenggang Ying
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying the interactivity of quantum instruments is fundamental to understanding their resource structure and operational capabilities. Here, we introduce the interactive weight of quantum instruments as a resource quantifier that measures the minimum fraction of an instrument that cannot be explained by non-interactive components. Through quantum-information tasks including quantum-state recovery, positive linear loss games, and environment-assisted input-blind extraction, we establish quantitative bounds on the interactive weight of quantum instruments and exact operational characterizations of its complementary quantity, the maximal non-interactive content. In particular, we extend environment-assisted input-blind extraction to the setting of restricted environmental access and develop a corresponding framework. Within the allowed-operations framework introduced by Hsieh et al., we establish fundamental resource-theoretic properties of the interactive weight of quantum instruments, including faithfulness, convexity, and monotonicity under deterministic allowed operations. Furthermore, we prove that the maximal non-interactive content satisfies exact multiplicativity under independent parallel composition, yielding necessary constraints on multicopy resource conversion and establishing the finite-copy maximal-weight distillation no-go result under deterministic allowed operations. These results establish a unified theoretical framework for the interactive weight of quantum instruments from the perspectives of resource quantification, operational interpretation, and resource conversion, providing systematic theoretical tools for the quantitative comparison and conversion of interactive quantum instruments.

motivation: Quantifying how much a quantum instrument is genuinely interactive is fundamental for understanding its resource structure and operational capabilities.
method: The authors define the interactive weight as the minimum fraction of an instrument not explainable by non-interactive components, derive bounds via quantum-state recovery, positive linear loss games, and environment-assisted input-blind extraction, and develop resource-theoretic monotonicity and multiplicativity results.
result: They obtain quantitative bounds and exact operational characterizations of maximal non-interactive content, prove faithfulness, convexity, and monotonicity under allowed operations, and establish exact multiplicativity plus a finite-copy maximal-weight distillation no-go result.
conclusion: The work provides a unified framework for quantifying, interpreting, and comparing interactive quantum instruments, with implications for multicopy resource conversion.

title: Threshold-Free Symmetry-Enriched Topological Quantum Memory
authors: Abhijat Sarma, Ruochen Ma, Cenke Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that non-Abelian symmetry enrichment can protect a toric code memory against incoherent electric noise at any bond error probability [MATH]. For a toric code on the honeycomb lattice coupled to [MATH] rotors, with electric anyons carrying the fundamental representation, we construct an efficient minimum-weight decoder whose logical error probability decays exponentially with system size for [MATH], a conservative sufficient bound. The same decoder also rules out strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking in the fundamental channel of [MATH] under the corresponding local decoherence in two dimensions. The construction extends to other symmetries, including [MATH].

title: Information-Spectrum General Formulas For The Capacity Region Of Classical-Quantum Multiple Access Channels
authors: Hiroshi Nagaoka Takuya Kubo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For classical-quantum multiple access channels (cq-MACs) with two senders, we give several general expressions for the capacity region, valid for arbitrary sequences of channels. In the case of asymptotically vanishing error ([MATH]), the capacity region is expressed in terms of spectral inf-mutual information rates. For every [MATH], the [MATH]-capacity region is expressed in terms of a quantity defined through a linear combination of three alternative hypotheses. In particular, the outer bound of Kubo and Nagaoka (2015) is tight. Our results include the quantum counterpart of the general formula of Han (1998) for the classical MAC. The most important ingredient is the one-shot inner bound of Sen (2021), which we apply to each member of an arbitrary channel sequence.
tldr: The paper derives general information-spectrum formulas for the capacity region of classical-quantum multiple access channels valid for arbitrary channel sequences.
motivation: Capacity regions for classical-quantum multiple access channels are less understood than their classical counterparts, and the authors aim to provide general formulas analogous to Han's classical information-spectrum results.
method: The authors use information-spectrum techniques, expressing capacity regions via spectral inf-mutual information rates and applying Sen's one-shot inner bound to each member of an arbitrary channel sequence.
result: They obtain general expressions for the capacity region under asymptotically vanishing error and for the epsilon-capacity region, showing that the Kubo-Nagaoka outer bound is tight and recovering the quantum counterpart of Han's formula.
conclusion: The work establishes a general information-spectrum framework for cq-MAC capacity regions, extending classical results and clarifying tightness of known bounds.

title: Single-shot Ground-state Preparation Via Strongly Coupled Baths
authors: Liang-Hong Mo, Jerome Lloyd, Yuxuan Zhang, Dmitry A. Abanin, Biao Lian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preparing ground and thermal states of quantum many-body systems is a central task in quantum simulation. Dissipative protocols have emerged as a promising solution for both near-term and fault-tolerant hardware, but most constructions rely on weak system-bath coupling, leading to slow cooling. Here, we construct cooling protocols at strong system-bath coupling, and demonstrate accurate state preparation within even a single cooling cycle. Our protocols combine dynamically ramped ancilla energy levels with time-dependent couplings to optimize the trade-off between cooling error and physical time. For a general class of free-fermion systems, we reduce the dynamics exactly to a two-level scattering problem: ground-state cooling becomes a control problem of maximizing resonant excitation transfer while suppressing non-adiabatic heating. We then construct a family of ``M\"obius-Ingham'' protocols, which reach optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and almost-exponential suppression of the leading heating error for gapped spectra, as a function of the cycle period. In our free-fermion benchmarks, M\"obius-Ingham cooling lies on the Pareto frontier between steady-state error and cooling time among the controls tested. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in interacting Ising and [MATH]-[MATH] chains and the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. Finally, we extend our construction to Gibbs state preparation, showing how free-fermion thermal states can be prepared in a single cycle.

motivation: Most dissipative state-preparation schemes rely on weak system-bath coupling, which makes cooling slow; this work aims to achieve accurate state preparation faster by operating at strong coupling.
method: The authors design dynamically ramped ancilla levels and time-dependent couplings, exactly reduce free-fermion dynamics to a two-level scattering problem, and construct Möbius-Ingham protocols optimizing resonant transfer versus non-adiabatic heating.
result: The protocols achieve optimal error scaling for gapless spectra and almost-exponential suppression of heating for gapped spectra, lying on the Pareto frontier of steady-state error versus cooling time in free-fermion benchmarks, and they also work for interacting Ising, XXZ-like chains, and the 2D Fermi-Hubbard model.
conclusion: Strongly coupled baths enable single-shot ground-state and Gibbs-state preparation, providing a practical route for dissipative quantum simulation and state engineering.

title: Efficient Pauli Truncation From Operator Stabilizer R\'enyi Entropy
authors: Yongming Li Haihui Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Operator stabilizer R\'enyi entropy (OSE) quantifies the magic of Heisenberg operators and serves as a diagnostic of their compressibility in the Pauli basis. We establish rigorous bounds showing when an operator can be efficiently approximated by Pauli truncation in terms of the scaling of its OSE. Specifically, we prove that volume-law scaling of OSE for [MATH] prevents efficient Pauli truncation from reproducing expectation values for all states at sufficiently small fixed error. On the other hand, logarithmic growth of OSE for [MATH] guarantees efficient Pauli truncation approximability uniformly over all states. A counterexample shows that this sufficient range cannot be extended on the basis of OSE scaling alone. If we restrict to correlations over suitable low-average state ensembles, then the sufficient range extends to [MATH]. We further derive cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation and approximation guarantees for fixed-order out-of-time-ordered correlators. Moreover, under an independent-sign assumption, we show that logarithmic OSE for [MATH] guarantees efficient Pauli truncation with the prescribed accuracy for all input states with high probability. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding when operator magic constrains or enables efficient Pauli truncation and for guiding the development of classical simulation methods.

method: The authors prove bounds connecting volume-law, logarithmic, and intermediate OSE scaling to uniform approximability by Pauli truncation, including cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation and fixed-order OTOC approximation guarantees.

conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework showing how operator magic constrains or enables efficient Pauli truncation, with implications for classical simulation methods and resource-theoretic analysis.

title: Uniform Three-Fold Product Expansion Of Algebraic-Geometry Codes Over A Fixed Field
authors: Min-Hsiu Hsieh Cassie Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A collection of classical codes [MATH] has product expansion if every low-weight word in the sum of their extensions to the product space can be written as a sum of words supported on few lines, each line being a codeword of the corresponding [MATH]. No explicit family over a fixed field was previously known to achieve constant rate, linear distance for both the code and its dual, and 3-fold product expansion at growing length. We prove that for the one-point evaluation codes [MATH] of length [MATH] and pole order [MATH] on the Garcia--Stichtenoth tower over [MATH], the triple [MATH] has product expansion with a constant independent of [MATH]. The dual codes [MATH] then form an explicit fixed-field family of rate tending to [MATH] and relative distance at least [MATH]. The proof is geometric: we view the words of the sum code as arrays on the product of three copies of the [MATH]-th curve of the tower, where the parity checks are sections of a line bundle. An exact generation theorem describes the sum-code words supported on the grid footprint of a suitable divisor. A support-localisation argument then shows that every low-weight array lies on such a divisor, after deleting a small number of coordinates. We also give a sufficient criterion for three-fold product expansion in terms of degree and genus ratios, yielding explicit families over every non-prime finite field of order at least [MATH]. method: The authors study one-point evaluation codes on the Garcia--Stichtenoth tower over a fixed finite field and prove product expansion geometrically by viewing sum-code words as arrays on a product of curves, using an exact generation theorem and a support-localisation argument.

title: Improving Gravitationally Induced Entanglement In Interferometric Configurations
authors: Alireza Maleki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proposals to detect gravitationally induced entanglement between massive particles offer a promising pathway toward probing the quantum nature of gravity. We perform a systematic geometric optimization and comparative analysis of Stern--Gerlach (SG) and Mach--Zehnder (MZ) matter-wave interferometers for this purpose, deriving exact analytical expressions for the gravitational phase of each configuration. Our first key result is that geometric optimization is indispensable. For commonly assumed experimental parameters, neglecting the optimization of geometric ratios can suppress the accumulated phase, and hence the detectability of entanglement, by up to several orders of magnitude. Second, we provide a complete comparative analysis of two SG orientations (linear and parallel) and three MZ orientations (translation-symmetric, mirror-symmetric, and parallel-arms). The parallel-arms SG and MZ configurations tend to yield the largest phase accumulations and are nearly equivalent in performance, whereas the translation-symmetric MZ setup exhibits destructive-interference nulls that act as blind operating points where detection becomes ineffective. These observations highlight the importance of geometry-aware design. A Monte Carlo error analysis of realistic fabrication tolerances indicates that the parallel-arms configurations are generally more robust, maintaining low relative phase uncertainty over broad parameter intervals. Furthermore, an evaluation of Bell violations assesses the feasibility and signal-to-noise ratio of each configuration. Our results identify geometric optimization, particularly through parallel-arms designs, as an important consideration for near-term experiments targeting gravitationally induced entanglement.
tldr: The paper optimizes interferometer geometries to enhance the detectability of gravitationally induced entanglement and evaluates Bell violation feasibility.
motivation: Detecting gravitationally induced entanglement offers a route to probing the quantum nature of gravity, but experimental signals are extremely weak and sensitive to geometry.
method: The author derives exact gravitational phases for Stern-Gerlach and Mach-Zehnder matter-wave interferometers, systematically compares orientations, and performs Monte Carlo error analysis under realistic fabrication tolerances.
result: Geometric optimization can increase the accumulated phase by orders of magnitude; parallel-arms configurations generally yield the largest and most robust signals, while translation-symmetric MZ setups exhibit destructive-interference nulls.
conclusion: Geometry-aware design, especially parallel-arms interferometers, is important for near-term experiments aiming to detect gravitationally induced entanglement and Bell violations.

title: Spin-Exchange-Controlled Nonclassical Light In Cavity Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
authors: Jing Tang, Junyu Su, Jie Chen, Ziyang Li, Yuangang Deng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlling nonclassical light while maintaining a finite cavity response requires selective suppression of unwanted multiphoton excitation. We investigate a ring-cavity system containing two three-level emitters coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, where electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) provides resonant access to a dark-state polariton. The exchange interaction shifts the polariton resonance while modifying the dressed two-photon excitation pathways. Strong photon antibunching emerges when the one-polariton resonance nearly coincides with a destructive-interference minimum of the second-photon transition amplitude. By jointly tuning the exchange interaction and control-field strength, pronounced photon blockade with a finite intracavity population can be sustained over an extended interaction range. We further show that the relative cavity-coupling phase redistributes optical coupling between symmetric and antisymmetric collective channels with opposite exchange shifts, allowing the photon statistics to switch between antibunching and bunching at fixed exchange strength. This mechanism provides a possible route to tunable nonclassical-light sources based on coherent control of collective excitation pathways.
tldr: A ring-cavity EIT system with two three-level emitters coupled by coherent spin exchange is shown to produce tunable photon blockade and switchable antibunching/bunching via the exchange strength, control-field amplitude, and cavity-coupling phase.
motivation: Maintaining a finite cavity response while suppressing unwanted multiphoton excitation is a central obstacle for deterministic nonclassical light sources; the authors ask whether a coherent spin-exchange interaction can serve as an extra knob to control the dressed two-photon pathways in cavity EIT.
method: They model a ring cavity containing two three-level emitters with a coherent spin-exchange coupling, using the EIT dark-state polariton picture and computing the dressed two-photon transition amplitudes and second-order coherence g(2) as functions of exchange strength, control field, and cavity-coupling phase.

conclusion: Coherent control of collective excitation pathways via spin exchange offers a viable route to tunable, phase-switchable nonclassical-light sources in cavity-EIT platforms.

Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with [MATH]. The unrounded bounds differ by less than [MATH]. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.

title: Higher-order Topological Quantum Battery
authors: Motohiko Ezawa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum battery is a next-generation energy-storage device that exploits genuinely quantum properties such as superposition and coherence. We propose a second-order topological quantum battery coupled to a photonic crystal described by the breathing-Kagome model, where optical loss is present on all lattice sites while nonlinear gains are introduced selectively at the output sites. Under these realistic non-Hermitian conditions, the system exhibits a clear topological phase transition manifested in both the ergotropy and the charging power. Remarkably, perfect work extraction is realized in the topological phase, where the maximum value of the ergotropy is quantized and acts as a good topological-phase indicator. The triangular geometry coherently distributes energy into two quantum batteries, where mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization gives rise to collective energy storage.
tldr: The paper proposes a second-order topological quantum battery in a non-Hermitian breathing-Kagome photonic crystal, showing that topological phases enable quantized ergotropy and enhanced charging power.
motivation: Quantum batteries aim to exploit quantum coherence and superposition for energy storage, and topological robustness may provide a route to stable and efficient work extraction under realistic lossy conditions.
method: The author couples a quantum battery to a photonic crystal described by the breathing-Kagome model with uniform optical loss and selective nonlinear gain at output sites, then analyzes the non-Hermitian topological phase transition via ergotropy and charging power.
result: Perfect work extraction occurs in the topological phase, where the maximum ergotropy is quantized and serves as a topological-phase indicator; mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization enables collective energy storage across two batteries.
conclusion: Higher-order topology can provide a robust design principle for quantum batteries, linking topological phase transitions to quantized thermodynamic performance under non-Hermitian conditions.

title: Particle-loss Error Correction Using $2^l$-step States Generated Via Particle-number-resolving Measurement Schemes
authors: E. A. Nesterova S. B. Korolev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an iterative scheme for generating finite superpositions of Fock states whose photon numbers differ by [MATH] ([MATH]-step states). We derive an upper bound on the probability of generating such states. Based on the proposed class of states, we construct several bosonic encodings and compare their performance in correcting particle-loss errors. Our results identify the most efficient encoding, which achieves a higher channel fidelity than previously studied bosonic encodings.

title: Dithered Belief Propagation For Real-Time Quantum Memory Decoding
authors: Zhengyu Cai, Mohamad Ali Jarkas, Bokun Zhao, Warren J. Gross
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce dithered belief-propagation decoding for circuit-level quantum memory to mitigate the oscillations and trapping behavior that limit standard belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes. Our approach combines a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation. Evaluated under circuit-level noise on the distance-11 rotated surface code and the distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, the proposed dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. The proposed decoder achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while trading a moderate increase in additions for about 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminating node-level RNGs. These results suggest that dithering is a promising approach toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.
tldr: The paper introduces a dithered belief-propagation decoder for circuit-level quantum memory that mitigates trapping and oscillation, matching Relay-BP accuracy with far fewer multiplications.
motivation: Standard belief-propagation decoders for quantum LDPC codes suffer from oscillations and trapping sets under circuit-level noise, and existing fixes such as BP+OSD or Relay-BP carry high computational cost that hinders real-time operation.
method: The authors augment BP with a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism plus chained randomized prior perturbation (dithering), replacing node-level random number generators with structured perturbations, and benchmark it on a distance-11 rotated surface code and a distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code under circuit-level noise.
result: The dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10, matches or exceeds Relay-BP especially at higher physical error rates, and achieves roughly 98% fewer multiplications on average with no node-level RNGs at the cost of moderately more additions.
conclusion: Dithering is a promising low-complexity route toward real-time decoding of quantum memories built on qLDPC codes.

title: Upper And Lower Bounds For Few-copy Gaussian Tomography, And The Absence Of A Fermionic Warm Regime
authors: Ron Rubin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill proved a crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography: cold states need [MATH] copies under single-copy or few-copy measurements, warm ones [MATH]. The author proved [MATH] for adaptive single-copy tomography of mixed fermionic Gaussian states. This note shows the crossover has no fermionic counterpart and extends the fermionic bound to blocks of [MATH] copies. There is no warm regime: on the quadratic Gibbs balls [MATH] of unknown Hamiltonian [MATH], the single-copy rate is [MATH] for every fixed [MATH], at accuracies that resolve the ball, with a lower-bound constant independent of [MATH]. At the maximally mixed state a replicated-parameter Fisher budget gives [MATH] for blocks of at most [MATH] copies and all [MATH]; an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information, via spinor tensor powers of [MATH], shows that the budget [MATH] behind it is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size; whether [MATH] is the true rate is open. Near the vacuum, block protocols need [MATH] copies, with no logarithm, via an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography; parity superselection changes no rate, and number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs. The embedding also carries upper bounds: a particle-number measurement followed by the [MATH]-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou attains the lower bound for every [MATH] on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states with bounded fugacity trace and on passive bosonic Gaussian states with bounded photon number, and a heterodyne stage that undoes displacement and squeezing extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states. tldr: This note establishes upper and lower bounds for few-copy Gaussian quantum tomography and shows that the bosonic cold/warm tomography crossover has no fermionic analogue.
motivation: Prior work by Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill found a copy-complexity crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography, and the author asks whether fermionic Gaussian states exhibit a corresponding warm regime.
method: The paper derives adaptive single-copy and block few-copy tomography bounds using Fisher-information budgets, spinor tensor powers, exterior-power embeddings, and reductions to qudit tomography protocols.
result: It finds no fermionic warm regime: on quadratic Gibbs balls the single-copy rate is constant for every fixed accuracy, and near the vacuum block protocols require a number of copies without a logarithmic factor; matching upper bounds are obtained via particle-number measurements and heterodyne stage.
conclusion: The fermionic few-copy tomography bound is extended to blocks of copies and the cold bosonic entangled-copy gap is closed, while intermediate-temperature cases remain open.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates quantum tomography of fermionic Gaussian states, focusing on the sample complexity of learning an unknown quadratic Hamiltonian h that defines a Gibbs state. Prior work by Chen, Mele, Mele, and Preskill established a crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography: cold states require Θ(m^3/ε^2) copies, while warm states require only Θ(m^2/ε^2). The author previously proved an Ω(m^3/ε^2) lower bound for adaptive single-copy tomography of mixed fermionic Gaussian states. Here, the author shows that no such crossover exists for fermions: on the quadratic Gibbs balls β||h||_F ≤ β0, the single-copy rate is Θ(m^3/ε^2) for every fixed β0 > 0, with a lower-bound constant independent of β0. The paper extends the lower bound to measurements on blocks of k copies, proving that at the maximally mixed state, N > m^3/(8,553,600 k ε^2) for blocks of at most k copies and all ε ≤ 1/3600. An exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information is derived via spinor tensor powers of so(2m), showing that the budget mt^2 is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size. Near the vacuum, block protocols need Ω(m^3/(ε^2 min{√k, m})) copies, with no logarithmic factor, using an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography. The paper also shows that parity superselection does not change the rate, and number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs. Upper bounds are provided: a particle-number measurement followed by the k-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou attains the lower bound for every k on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states with bounded fugacity trace and on passive bosonic Gaussian states with bounded photon number. A heterodyne stage extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states, closing the k-entangled gap on the cold class, while intermediate temperatures remain open.

Extends the fermionic lower bound to measurements on blocks of k copies, showing that at the maximally mixed state, N > m^3/(8,553,600 k ε^2) for all ε ≤ 1/3600, and derives an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information via spinor tensor powers of so(2m).

For the lower bounds, the author uses Fisher information techniques, specifically analyzing the maximal block Fisher information for measurements on k copies. This allows the author to show that the Fisher information budget mt^2 is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size. title: Logically Augmented Quantum Ldpc Codes: Construction And Hierarchical Decoding
authors: Sheida Rabeti, Ayushi Shirke, Ivana Dimitrova, Hessam Mahdavifar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a joint framework for constructing and decoding Logically Augmented (LA) quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. This is motivated by the need for flexible coding rates and adaptive error protection while preserving block length and code structure. On the construction side, we use an auxiliary to impose additional stabilizer constraints on selected logical qubits of a code. On the decoding side, the proposed decoder uses the LPC syndrome to generate logical error hypotheses and condition belief propagation (BP) on each hypothesis. The proposed is invoked only when the initial BP decoder for primary code fails to converge. It then selects the correction with the smallest Hamming weight among the syndrome-consistent candidates produced by hypothesis-conditioned BP runs. For numerical evaluation, we focus on short repetition LPCs, which provide a flexible means of trading rate for additional error protection. Each LPC syndrome admits exactly two logical error hypotheses, irrespective of repetition length, which enables HLLD to explore both possibilities without relying on a single logical estimate. Numerical results show that varying the repetition length provides a tunable trade-off between rate and error-correction performance across a wide range of primary code constructions and their operating regimes. On the decoding side, with the overall LA code held fixed, HLLD reduces the logical error rate by up to 81\%, 75\%, and 69\% for LA codes based on mitten, lifted-product, and bivariate bicycle codes, respectively, compared with conventional BP decoding of the same LA codes.
tldr: The paper proposes a joint construction and decoding framework for logically augmented quantum LDPC codes that adds stabilizer constraints to selected logical qubits and uses hypothesis-conditioned belief propagation for decoding.
motivation: The work aims to provide flexible coding rates and adaptive error protection for QLDPC codes while preserving block length and code structure.
method: An auxiliary code imposes additional stabilizer constraints on chosen logical qubits, and a hierarchical decoder generates logical error hypotheses from the LPC syndrome and conditions BP runs on each hypothesis, selecting the lowest-weight syndrome-consistent correction.
result: For short repetition LPCs, each syndrome yields exactly two logical error hypotheses, and the hierarchical decoder reduces logical error rates by up to 81%, 75%, and 69% for LA codes based on mitten, lifted-product, and bivariate bicycle codes, respectively, compared with conventional BP decoding.
conclusion: Logically augmented QLDPC codes with hierarchical decoding offer a tunable rate-versus-protection trade-off and significant decoding improvements across several primary code families.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a joint framework for constructing and decoding Logically Augmented (LA) quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes, aiming to provide flexible coding rates and adaptive error protection while preserving block length and code structure. On the construction side, an auxiliary Logical Protection Code (LPC) imposes additional stabilizer constraints on selected logical qubits of a primary code. On the decoding side, a Hierarchical Logical List Decoder (HLLD) is introduced: it uses the LPC syndrome to generate logical error hypotheses and conditions belief propagation (BP) on each hypothesis. HLLD is invoked only when the initial BP decoder for the primary code fails to converge, and it selects the correction with the smallest Hamming weight among syndrome-consistent candidates from hypothesis-conditioned BP runs. The numerical evaluation focuses on short repetition LPCs, which provide a tunable trade-off between rate and error-correction performance. Each LPC syndrome admits exactly two logical error hypotheses regardless of repetition length, enabling HLLD to explore both possibilities without relying on a single logical estimate. Results show that varying the repetition length tunes the rate-performance trade-off across various primary code constructions. With the overall LA code fixed, HLLD reduces the logical error rate by up to 81%, 75%, and 69% for LA codes based on mitten, lifted-product, and bivariate bicycle codes, respectively, compared to conventional BP decoding of the same LA codes.

Demonstration that short repetition LPCs yield exactly two logical error hypotheses per syndrome, allowing efficient exploration of both possibilities without relying on a single logical estimate.

Numerical evaluation showing tunable rate-performance trade-offs via repetition length and significant logical error rate reductions (up to 81%, 75%, and 69% for mitten, lifted-product, and bivariate bicycle codes, respectively) compared to conventional BP decoding of the same LA codes.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines code construction and decoding innovation. Construction: An LPC is applied to selected logical qubits of a primary QLDPC code, adding stabilizer constraints that effectively create a hierarchical code structure. This allows the overall code to maintain the same block length and structure while varying the protection level through the LPC's parameters (e.g., repetition length). Decoding: The HLLD operates in two stages. First, standard BP decoding is attempted on the primary code. If it converges, the correction is accepted. If not, the LPC syndrome is used to generate a list of logical error hypotheses (for repetition LPCs, exactly two hypotheses). For each hypothesis, BP is run with the hypothesis as a condition (likely by modifying the syndrome or prior probabilities). The resulting candidate corrections that are consistent with the full syndrome are collected, and the one with the smallest Hamming weight is selected. This approach leverages the additional information from the LPC to disambiguate logical errors that cause BP to fail, without significantly increasing complexity since HLLD is only invoked on failure.
deep_read.results_analysis: The numerical results focus on short repetition LPCs and demonstrate two key findings. First, varying the repetition length provides a tunable trade-off between coding rate and error-correction performance across a wide range of primary code constructions and operating regimes. This flexibility is valuable for adapting to varying noise levels or resource constraints. Second, with the overall LA code fixed, HLLD significantly outperforms conventional BP decoding of the same LA code, reducing the logical error rate by up to 81% for mitten codes, 75% for lifted-product codes, and 69% for bivariate bicycle codes. These improvements are attributed to the hypothesis-conditioned BP runs that explore multiple logical error possibilities, avoiding the pitfalls of a single logical estimate. The results are presented for short repetition LPCs, which are practical due to their simplicity and the exactly-two-hypotheses property.

The framework is modular: the LPC can be chosen based on desired trade-offs, and the decoder can be applied to any primary code, making it broadly applicable.
limitations: The evaluation is limited to short repetition LPCs; other LPC choices (e.g., more complex codes) may offer different trade-offs but are not explored, leaving the generality of the approach untested.

The decoder's performance is compared only to conventional BP decoding of the same LA code, not to other advanced decoders (e.g., ordered statistics decoding or other list decoders), so the relative advantage over state-of-the-art is unclear.
The paper does not provide a theoretical analysis of the achievable rate-performance trade-off or the conditions under which HLLD guarantees improvement, relying instead on numerical evidence.

title: Elimination Of Quantum Causal Confusion In The Presence Of Dual States
authors: Weixiang Ye James Fullwood
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There is a rich class of bipartite quantum correlations between qubits which are consistent both with measurements performed in parallel and measurements performed in sequence. This phenomenon has recently been termed , which is made mathematically precise by the notion of a dual state---a bipartite density operator whose associated correlations are causally ambiguous. A natural question is then whether or not the spatial and temporal scenarios associated with a dual state are fundamentally indistinguishable from a causal perspective. Here we show that as long as the reduced density operator of a dual state is oblique---meaning that all coefficients in its Pauli expansion are non-zero---then the underlying joint probabilities giving rise to such causally ambiguous correlations will differ in the spatial and temporal scenarios. Specifically, the temporal joint probabilities will inherently violate the no-signalling condition, thus eliminating quantum causal confusion. Moreover, as oblique states form an open dense subset of the Bloch ball, the elimination of quantum causal confusion is the norm rather than an exception.
tldr: The paper shows that for dual states whose reduced density operator is oblique, the spatial and temporal joint probabilities differ because the temporal probabilities violate no-signalling, thereby eliminating quantum causal confusion.
motivation: Dual states produce bipartite quantum correlations that are consistent with both parallel and sequential measurement scenarios, raising the question of whether the spatial and temporal causal interpretations are fundamentally indistinguishable.
method: The authors analyze the Pauli expansion of the reduced density operator of a dual state and prove that obliqueness—all Pauli coefficients nonzero—forces the temporal joint probabilities to violate the no-signalling condition.
result: Quantum causal confusion is eliminated whenever the reduced state is oblique, and since oblique states form an open dense subset of the Bloch ball, this elimination is generic rather than exceptional.
conclusion: Causally ambiguous correlations from dual states are typically distinguishable across spatial and temporal scenarios, making quantum causal confusion a non-generic phenomenon.

title: Information Flow Control In Hybrid Quantum Networks
authors: Michael Siomau
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum resources can change the dynamical features and operational behaviors of conventional networks. Long-distance entanglement supports information transfer between nodes lacking a direct connection. This entanglement link not only modifies the stationary effective connectivity of the network but can also be used to suppress undesirable classical dynamics. By examining information flow control mechanism, we demonstrate that classical collective behavior can be well-balanced by altering the initially distributed entanglement. We show the entanglement thresholds for two distinct control approaches: linear response control and Lyapunov functional controllability.
tldr: The paper shows that tuning distributed entanglement in hybrid quantum networks can control information flow and balance classical collective dynamics, with thresholds derived for two control strategies.
motivation: Quantum resources such as long-distance entanglement can alter network connectivity and dynamics, motivating the use of entanglement as a control mechanism for undesirable classical behavior in hybrid networks.
method: The author analyzes an information-flow control mechanism and derives entanglement thresholds for linear-response control and Lyapunov-functional controllability.
result: Classical collective behavior can be balanced by changing the initially distributed entanglement, and the two control approaches have distinct entanglement thresholds.
conclusion: Entanglement distribution provides a controllable resource for regulating information flow and network dynamics, suggesting design principles for hybrid quantum networks.

title: A Wigner-Lindblad Phase Space Model For Open Quantum Dynamics
authors: O. Morandi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the collisional quantum dynamics of an open system in contact with a thermal bath. We propose a particle-bath interaction model based on the Weyl quantization principle and the Wigner phase space description of quantum evolution. By factorizing the reduced Hamiltonian of the open system via supersymmetric quantum mechanics techniques, we construct system-dependent creation and annihilation operators for arbitrary potential landscapes. This allows us to extend the classical Fokker--Planck relaxation mechanism to incorporate Lindblad quantum stochastic jumps within the Wigner phase-space formalism. Through a semiclassical expansion of the Moyal star product to second order, we obtain a generalized Wigner--Lindblad kinetic model featuring position-dependent friction and diffusion terms. We establish the mathematical well-posedness of the Lindblad problem and we validate our approach through numerical simulations. Our model resolves unphysical long-time artifacts of standard quantum Fokker--Planck models in quartic double-well traps, accurately captures dissipative quantum state localization in 2D molecular potentials (4D phase space), and effectively evaluates electron transport and trapping times in InAs/InP resonant tunneling diodes.
tldr: The paper develops a Wigner-Lindblad phase-space model for open quantum systems coupled to a thermal bath, combining Weyl quantization, supersymmetric factorization, and semiclassical Moyal expansion.
motivation: Standard quantum Fokker-Planck models can produce unphysical long-time artifacts, motivating a more consistent phase-space description of dissipative quantum dynamics with Lindblad jumps.
method: The authors construct system-dependent creation/annihilation operators via supersymmetric quantum mechanics, extend Fokker-Planck relaxation to Lindblad stochastic jumps in Wigner phase space, and derive a generalized Wigner-Lindblad kinetic model with position-dependent friction and diffusion.
result: The model is shown to be mathematically well-posed and numerically validated; it resolves long-time artifacts in quartic double wells, captures dissipative localization in 2D molecular potentials, and estimates electron transport/trapping times in InAs/InP resonant tunneling diodes.
conclusion: The work provides a phase-space framework for open quantum dynamics and quantum transport, but its contribution is primarily methodological rather than centered on information-thermodynamic bounds or information-theoretic results.

title: Quantum Communication And Phase Sensing Over A Dephasing Channel With Thermal Noise
authors: Ioannis Krikidis Nikos A. Mitsiou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dephasing is a prominent source of decoherence in quantum communication, degrading phase coherence and transmission reliability. Therefore, knowledge of the physical channel parameters for reliable transmission is imperative, motivating the integration of quantum communication and sensing at the physical layer. Consequently, we study the transmission of coherent states over a von Mises dephasing channel affected by thermal noise. We consider a heterodyne receiver, for which, we first derive the symbol-error probability (SEP) and an accurate closed-form approximation, through which an irreducible asymptotic error floor due to the dephasing channel is identified. We note that the derived SEP is affected by the mismatch between the receiver's mean phase estimation and the true mean phase, thereby formalizing the interplay between sensing accuracy and communication reliability. In addition, we derive the Fisher information (FI) for the mean phase acquisition of the channel and provide closed-form lower and upper FI bounds. Moreover, the quantum FI (QFI) of the channel is studied, and lower and upper bounds on the QFI are given, which become asymptotically tight as the photon number increases. Despite the initial complexity of the FI and the QFI, the bounds given are relatively simple and effective. In addition, by comparing the FI with the QFI, we show that heterodyne detection approaches the quantum sensing limit as the number of photons increase, while an unavoidable sensing floor exists due to dephasing. Then, using the SEP and the FI analysis, we discuss the conditions under which communication and phase estimation requirements are jointly feasible. Finally, numerical results validate the derived SEP, estimation bounds, and the sensing-communication feasibility tradeoff.
tldr: The paper analyzes coherent-state transmission over a von Mises dephasing channel with thermal noise, deriving symbol-error probability and Fisher-information bounds for joint communication and phase sensing.
motivation: Dephasing degrades phase coherence in quantum communication, so reliable transmission benefits from estimating channel phase and integrating quantum sensing with communication at the physical layer.
method: The authors consider a heterodyne receiver, derive the symbol-error probability and a closed-form approximation, and compute classical and quantum Fisher information with lower and upper bounds for mean-phase estimation.
result: They identify an irreducible asymptotic error floor due to dephasing, formalize the impact of phase-estimation mismatch on communication reliability, and show that heterodyne detection approaches the quantum sensing limit as photon number increases, while a dephasing-induced sensing floor remains.
conclusion: The work characterizes a feasibility tradeoff between communication reliability and phase-sensing accuracy over a noisy dephasing channel, with numerical results validating the derived bounds.

title: FNO-Based Inverse Co-Design Of Semiconducting Quantum-Dot Devices
authors: Marek Rychetsky, Valentin Duruisseaux, Freya Shah, David L. Craig, Ming Ni, Georgios Katsaros, Taylor L. Patti, Anima Anandkumar, Natalia Ares
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots are promising building blocks for scalable spin-based quantum processors, however their operational properties depend on several fabrication and control parameters, such as lithographic gate layout and applied voltages. Existing device architectures have been refined through repeated fabrication and experimental testing, producing layouts that support reliable device operation. However, this process does not exhaustively explore the design space, limiting the ability to obtain qubits with targeted properties. We address these challenges by presenting a differentiable inverse co-design framework for electrostatically defined quantum dots that jointly optimises gate voltages and the gate electrode layout. A semiclassical Thomas--Fermi electrostatic simulator provides reference data for a Fourier neural operator (FNO) surrogate, which predicts the two-dimensional charge-density field. The desired spatial distribution of the confined charge defines the target quantum-dot geometry for inverse design. The FNO reproduces charge densities with a relative [MATH] test error of just 0.6\% and enables millisecond-scale differentiable evaluations. Relative to the CPU-based physics simulator, the FNO achieves a 17,000-fold speed-up on GPU for a single design, with further performance gains enabled by batched inference. When embedded in a gradient-based design loop with fabrication constraints, the FNO can produce both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot confinement geometries from the same initial conditions. The ability to engineer these distinct confinement configurations demonstrates control over quantum-dot shape and position, providing a route towards designing devices with distinct qubit-relevant operating properties prior to fabrication.
tldr: A differentiable inverse co-design framework using a Fourier neural operator surrogate of a Thomas–Fermi electrostatic simulator to jointly optimize gate voltages and gate layouts for gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots.
motivation: Gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots are promising for scalable spin qubits, but their properties depend on many fabrication and control parameters that are currently explored only through repeated fabrication and testing, leaving the design space largely unexplored.
method: A semiclassical Thomas–Fermi electrostatic simulator generates reference charge-density data, which trains an FNO surrogate achieving 0.6% relative error and millisecond-scale differentiable evaluation; this surrogate is embedded in a gradient-based optimization loop with fabrication constraints to jointly tune voltages and gate electrode geometry.
result: The FNO provides a 17,000-fold GPU speed-up over the CPU physics simulator and, within the design loop, produces both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot confinement geometries from the same initial conditions.
conclusion: The approach enables pre-fabrication engineering of quantum-dot shape and position, offering a route to designing devices with targeted qubit-relevant properties before fabrication.

title: Asymptotic Advantage Of Quantum One-way And Smp Communication For Total Functions
authors: Dmytro Gavinsky
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We exhibit a total Boolean function on n input bits whose bounded-error quantum simultaneous-message (and hence one-way) communication complexity is in O(\sqrt n), whereas its randomised one-way (and hence simultaneous-message) communication complexity is in \Omega(n). The same function admits a classical simultaneous-message protocol of cost O(\sqrt n) when the players share O(\sqrt n) EPR pairs.
tldr: A total Boolean function is constructed that separates bounded-error quantum simultaneous-message (and one-way) communication complexity, O(√n), from randomized one-way complexity, Ω(n), with a classical SMP protocol achieving O(√n) given O(√n) EPR pairs.
motivation: Communication complexity is a fundamental measure of the quantum advantage in distributed information processing, and separations for total functions are much harder to establish than for partial functions, making them valuable benchmarks.
method: Explicit construction of a total Boolean function together with upper and lower bound arguments: a quantum SMP protocol of cost O(√n), a randomized one-way lower bound of Ω(n), and an entanglement-assisted classical SMP protocol of cost O(√n).
result: An exponential-type separation between quantum and classical one-way/SMP communication complexity for a total function, showing that shared EPR pairs can reproduce the quantum advantage classically.
conclusion: The work sharpens the landscape of quantum versus classical communication complexity for total functions and highlights the power of shared entanglement in simultaneous-message settings.

title: Weak Values In Postselected Quantum Trajectories
authors: Janarbek Yuanbek, Yuan-De Jin, Wen-Long Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weak value (WV) describes the amplified response of a meter when the measured system undergoes postselection. While conventional WV theory mainly rests on a single system-meter interaction setting, it remains unexplored whether WV can act as an effective pointer for sequential quantum measurements under postselection. Here we introduce the concept of WVs to the setting of sequential quantum measurements and quantum trajectories. We find that WV naturally emerges in postselected quantum trajectories of sequential weak measurements, by establishing a connection between the WV of the measured observable and the postselected statistics of quantum trajectories. Using sequential weak measurements on a qubit or an oscillator implemented by Ramsey interferometry with an ancilla qubit, we show that postselection shifts the collective record polarization away from the unconditioned ones, with an effective bias described by the WV. Our predictions are feasible to test in various platforms.
tldr: The paper shows that weak values emerge as effective pointers in postselected quantum trajectories under sequential weak measurements.
motivation: Conventional weak-value theory mainly treats a single system-meter interaction, leaving open whether weak values can characterize sequential quantum measurements under postselection.
method: The authors introduce weak values into sequential weak measurements and quantum trajectories, connect the weak value of the measured observable to postselected trajectory statistics, and propose Ramsey interferometry with an ancilla qubit for qubit and oscillator implementations.
result: Postselection is found to shift the collective record polarization away from the unconditioned statistics, with an effective bias described by the weak value, and the predictions are feasible across several platforms.
conclusion: Weak values provide an effective pointer for postselected sequential measurement statistics, extending the weak-value formalism to quantum trajectories.

title: Bell Test And Quantum State-Space Geometry
authors: Michael Siomau
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We explore a minimal phenomenological model of coupling between the geometry of the classical spacetime and the quantum state space. Assuming a simple structure of the combined manifold, bilinear interaction between the corresponding geometric scalars and the simplest case of the two-qubit entanglement dynamics, we derive an illustrative upper bound on the geometric coupling constant from the requirement of the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality violation over a finite time interval.
tldr: The paper proposes a phenomenological model coupling classical spacetime geometry to quantum state-space geometry and uses CHSH violation to bound the coupling constant.
motivation: The author aims to explore a minimal model connecting spacetime geometry with quantum state space and to constrain such a coupling via a Bell-type inequality.
method: Assuming a simple combined manifold and bilinear interaction between geometric scalars, the study analyzes two-qubit entanglement dynamics and imposes CHSH violation over a finite time interval.
result: An illustrative upper bound on the geometric coupling constant is derived from the requirement that the CHSH inequality be violated.
conclusion: The work suggests a possible phenomenological link between spacetime geometry and quantum nonlocality, but it remains illustrative and does not advance core quantum information theory.

title: Scalable Transpilation For Overcoming Restricted Connectivity In Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
authors: Afonso Azenha, Ilia Polian, Sebastian Brandhofer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs [MATH] 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250[MATH] speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3[MATH]133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.
tldr: The paper introduces a scalable transpilation method for distributed superconducting quantum architectures with restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing promises to scale superconducting hardware, but limited connectivity and inefficient transpilation create major bottlenecks.
method: It combines a quantum interaction graph (QIG) graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic tailored to distributed architectures.
result: On 48-qubit and 399-qubit benchmarks, the method reduces aggregated costs by up to 24.72% versus DMapS and routing costs by up to 51.96% versus a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, with large speedups and practical runtimes.
conclusion: The work provides a practical transpilation approach for distributed quantum computing at scale, though it is primarily a compiler and architecture contribution rather than a networking protocol or information-theoretic result.
