title: Observing Mixed-state Uhlmann Winding Numbers In Integrated Photonic Quantum Walks
authors: Baichu Yu, Qin-Qin Wang, Huilong Huang, Bin-Tong Yin, Xiao-Ye Xu, Feng Gao, Xin Wang, Keren Li, Sen Yang, Yuan-Yuan Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integer winding numbers provide a well-established classification of topological phases protected by chiral symmetry at zero temperature, but extending this classification to thermal mixed states remains challenging. The Uhlmann phase, a mixed-state extension of the Berry phase, provides a geometric framework for characterizing finite-temperature topology. However, this geometric phase is restricted to two quantized values and therefore cannot resolve the multiple thermal regimes associated with high winding numbers. Here, we experimentally observe integer mixed-state winding numbers in a photonic quantum-walk chip. We prepare and reconstruct thermal states associated with high-winding chiral Hamiltonians and their spectrum-preserving dimensional extensions. The reconstructed Uhlmann overlaps form closed trajectories in the complex plane, and their integer windings around the zero-overlap point are directly observed. As temperature increases, the Uhlmann winding number undergoes multiple discrete changes, accompanied by switches of the Uhlmann phase and the successive disappearance of momentum-resolved topological kinks. These results highlight an integer-valued topological characterization alongside the mixed-state geometric phase.
tldr: The paper experimentally observes integer mixed-state Uhlmann winding numbers in integrated photonic quantum walks using reconstructed Uhlmann overlaps.
motivation: Extending integer winding-number classifications of chiral topological phases from pure ground states to thermal mixed states is challenging because the Uhlmann phase alone is restricted to two quantized values.
method: Thermal states associated with high-winding chiral Hamiltonians and spectrum-preserving dimensional extensions are prepared and reconstructed in a photonic quantum-walk chip, and Uhlmann overlaps are measured to form closed trajectories in the complex plane.
result: The integer winding of the Uhlmann overlap trajectories around the zero-overlap point is directly observed, with multiple discrete changes as temperature increases, accompanied by Uhlmann-phase switches and disappearance of momentum-resolved topological kinks.
conclusion: The work demonstrates an integer-valued topological characterization of mixed states alongside the mixed-state geometric phase, but its focus on topological phases and photonic quantum walks is not central to the researcher's quantum-information priorities.

title: A Complete Equational Theory For Quantum Circuits With Generalized Control
authors: Scott Wesley William Schober (universit\`a Della Svizzera Italiana)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlled subcircuits are commonplace in quantum algorithms as they represent the quantum analogue of branching statements (if then). We introduce a generalization of controlled subcircuits in the form of a binary operation which sends pairs of unitary quantum circuits to a generalized controlled operation, whose semantics are based on matrix exponentials and logarithms. The family of quantum circuits with generalized controlled operations and circuit exponentiation is denoted HQC for Hierarchical Quantum Circuits. We formalize HQC as a modified prop category using a novel category-theoretic construction, and provide a sound and complete equational theory for diagrammatic reasoning in HQC.
tldr: The paper introduces Hierarchical Quantum Circuits (HQC), a formalism extending quantum circuits with generalized controlled operations and circuit exponentiation, and provides a sound and complete equational theory for diagrammatic reasoning.
motivation: Controlled subcircuits are common in quantum algorithms, but standard controlled operations are limited; a more general notion based on matrix exponentials and logarithms could enable richer hierarchical circuit constructions.
method: The authors define a binary operation sending pairs of unitary quantum circuits to generalized controlled operations, formalize HQC as a modified prop category using a novel category-theoretic construction, and develop an equational theory for diagrammatic reasoning.
result: They obtain a sound and complete equational theory for HQC, enabling formal reasoning about circuits with generalized control and exponentiation.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational categorical framework and complete equational logic for hierarchical quantum circuits, advancing formal methods for quantum computation rather than directly addressing quantum information-theoretic questions.

title: Frustration-freeness Is Decidable But Unprovable
authors: Naoto Shiraishi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The frustration-free property is valuable in quantum many-body systems, which states that its ground states simultaneously minimize all local interaction terms, even when these terms act on overlapping degrees of freedom. Prominent examples include the AKLT model and Kitaev's toric code model, which serve as paradigmatic models of symmetry-protected topological phases and topological order, respectively. A fundamental question is whether a given Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes. Here we establish two seemingly contradictory results concerning this decision problem. First, we prove that frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension. Specifically, there exists a finite, Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff such that frustration-freeness at this cutoff size guarantees frustration-freeness at all system sizes. Second, on the other hand, we also show that there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC). We reconcile these seemingly contradictory results by showing that the cutoff, although finite for each local Hilbert space dimension, is uncomputable as a function of that dimension. Our findings reveal an unexpected fundamental distinction between decidability and provability arising in quantum many-body physics.
tldr: The paper proves that frustration-freeness of local Hamiltonians is decidable for fixed local dimension but can be unprovable in ZFC, with an uncomputable finite cutoff.
motivation: Frustration-free Hamiltonians are central in quantum many-body physics, but whether frustration-freeness can be decided for all system sizes is a fundamental computability question.
method: The author combines decidability arguments for local Hamiltonians with logical independence techniques from computability theory and ZFC.
result: For each fixed local Hilbert-space dimension there is a finite system-size cutoff guaranteeing frustration-freeness at all sizes, yet this cutoff is uncomputable as a function of the dimension, and some frustration-free Hamiltonians have ZFC-unprovable frustration-freeness.
conclusion: The work reveals a sharp distinction between decidability and provability in quantum many-body physics, with implications for the foundations of local Hamiltonian properties.

title: Structured Quantum Hardness From Unstructured Assumptions
authors: Xiao Liang, Takashi Yamakawa, Chak Fai Yung
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett-Gill question asks whether [MATH] remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if [MATH], then [MATH] with probability [MATH] over a random oracle [MATH]. Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor's algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources. Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in [MATH] to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.
tldr: The paper studies whether structured quantum hardness can arise from unstructured cryptographic assumptions, proving a conditional random-oracle separation and a black-box reduction barrier.
motivation: The Bennett-Gill question asks whether structured hardness can emerge from unstructured assumptions; the authors seek the quantum analogue relevant to post-quantum cryptography.
method: They establish a conditional oracle separation showing that certain structured quantum hardness exists relative to a random oracle under an assumption, and they rule out fully black-box quantum reductions from worst-case quantum hardness to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation.
result: The main result gives evidence that structured quantum hardness can arise from unstructured sources, while the barrier result shows that broad black-box approaches cannot derive such hardness from generic cryptographic primitives.
conclusion: The work extends classical complexity/cryptography results to the quantum setting and suggests that non-black-box techniques may be essential for obtaining structured quantum hardness from unstructured assumptions.

title: Physical Regimes Of Quartic Quantum Advantage In Elastic Media Simulation
authors: David Jennings, Kamil Korzekwa, Matteo Lostaglio, Tam\'as Vaszary
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum algorithms for elastic media simulation have been conjectured to offer up to a quartic quantum advantage over classical methods; however, the devil is always in the details. Here, we determine key physical conditions under which this quartic separation could be achieved in the relevant parameters. For continuum elastic dynamics at fixed volume with spatial convergence order [MATH], we find that the end-to-end speedup is of order [MATH] in the simulation time, and [MATH] in the accuracy, with exponential memory advantage. For elastic lattice systems, we define microscopically resolved bulk observables (MRBOs) as those that can be efficiently extracted from a quantum state, but cannot be resolved by a known continuum model with fewer degrees of freedom than the lattice. We then argue that the estimation of MRBOs is a candidate problem for quartic quantum advantage in problem size. We propose MRBOs for pseudorandom heterogeneous materials as an explicit end-to-end application where this occurs, while admitting efficient `quantum cheese' encodings of the material properties. We thus demonstrate how the interplay between regularity, physical scale, observable sensitivity and quantum encodability constrains the relation between classical and quantum complexity.
tldr: The paper identifies physical regimes and observable classes under which quantum algorithms for elastic media simulation could achieve quartic quantum advantage over classical methods.
motivation: Quantum algorithms for elastic media simulation have been conjectured to offer up to quartic speedups, but the physical and computational conditions required for this separation are unclear.
method: The authors analyze continuum elastic dynamics and lattice systems, define microscopically resolved bulk observables (MRBOs), and propose pseudorandom heterogeneous materials as an explicit end-to-end application with efficient quantum encodings.
result: For continuum dynamics with spatial convergence order, they find end-to-end speedups in simulation time and accuracy with exponential memory advantage; for lattice systems, MRBO estimation is argued to be a candidate for quartic quantum advantage in problem size.
conclusion: The interplay between regularity, physical scale, observable sensitivity, and quantum encodability constrains the relationship between classical and quantum complexity in elastic media simulation.

title: Langmuir Kinetics And Totally Asymmetric Volume Exclusion In Linear Chains Via Fock Space Formalism
authors: Luis D. S. Silva, Arthur M. S. Carvalho, Francisco A. G. Almeida, Gerson C. Duarte-Filho
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driven-diffusive systems combining spatial exclusion and bulk exchange, such as the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process coupled with Langmuir kinetics (TASEP-LK), serve as foundational models for particle transport in vehicular traffic, conveyor networks, and mesoscopic flow channels. In this work, we employ an exact Doi-Peliti field-theoretic operator formulation in Fock space to evaluate steady-state observables, continuous phase landscapes, and spatial correlations in finite linear chains up to [MATH]. By introducing a decomposition in terms of biorthonormal eigenvectors for asymmetric non-Hermitian matrices, the stationary state is calculated directly from the kernel of the quasi-Hamiltonian, completely bypassing the computationally prohibitive complexity of full matrix diagonalization and time-dependent matrix exponentiation. Across distinct rate regimes and global parametric scans, our exact discrete calculations demonstrate that finite-size stochastic fluctuations naturally smear out singular domain walls, producing smooth density profiles and continuous phase crossovers. Finite-size scaling illustrates how local profiles systematically steepen toward the sharp domain wall predicted by continuum field theory as [MATH]. Furthermore, two-point correlation analysis reveals that in slow-kinetics regimes, spatial fluctuations generate strong inter-site cumulants, causing standard mean-field approximations to systematically underestimate joint occupancy probabilities by 50\%. These findings emphasize the necessity of analytical methods for modeling mesoscopic transport systems and short traffic corridors where local stochastic fluctuations and spatial correlations dominate the stationary dynamics.
tldr: The paper develops an exact Fock-space Doi-Peliti formalism for steady-state properties of finite TASEP-LK chains, capturing finite-size fluctuations and spatial correlations.
motivation: Driven-diffusive systems such as TASEP with Langmuir kinetics are important models for transport, but exact finite-chain calculations are challenging due to non-Hermitian dynamics and strong correlations.
method: The authors use a Doi-Peliti operator formulation in Fock space and a biorthonormal eigenvector decomposition for asymmetric non-Hermitian matrices to compute stationary states without full diagonalization.
result: Exact discrete calculations show finite-size smoothing of domain walls, continuous phase crossovers, and strong inter-site cumulants in slow-kinetics regimes, with mean-field theory underestimating joint occupancies by up to 50%.
conclusion: The approach provides an efficient exact method for mesoscopic transport modeling and highlights the importance of stochastic fluctuations and correlations in finite linear chains.

title: Between Hi-Fi And Mmi: The Overlap Of Redundancy And Synergy In Partial Information Decomposition
authors: Niels van Santen, Yves Rosseel, Daniele Marinazzo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that two sources carry about a target into redundant, unique and synergistic parts, with nonnegative decompositions lying on a segment where redundancy measures are bounded by the positive part of the co-information and the smaller source-target information. We parameterize this segment by the overlap, the common excess of redundancy and synergy over their net balance, and show that for many of the named PID measures, their redundancy can be written as the largest positive part of the co-information over a set of reference distributions. This common form induces an ordering of those PIDs on the segment. With the smallest redundancy and synergy and the largest unique atoms of any nonnegative PID, the information-theoretic version of Hi-Fi, a feature-importance method, is the zero-overlap end of the segment for two sources, with the maximum overlap bound given by the minimum mutual information (MMI) PID. We introduce, by splitting the co-information into a pairwise maximum- entropy part and the third-order connected information, a PID that sits at zero overlap except when pairwise redundancy and triadic synergy coexist. For three or more sources the bivariate results hold on every pair of merged source groups, and among all nonnegative solutions of the lattice equations MMI and Hi-Fi still give the smallest and largest unique atoms but zero overlap on all pairs at once is often unattainable. Two inequalities across pairs are necessary in general and sufficient for three sources. For identity targets zero overlap is possible exactly when the sources' information diagram is nonnegative. In random three- and four-source distributions zero overlap on all pairs fails in 21-100% of the cases.
tldr: The paper analyzes partial information decomposition (PID) by parameterizing nonnegative redundancy-synergy tradeoffs via an overlap measure and deriving orderings among named PID measures.
motivation: PID lacks a unified understanding of how different redundancy measures relate, especially regarding the balance between redundancy and synergy in multivariate information decompositions.
method: The authors parameterize the segment of nonnegative PID solutions by overlap, express several named PID redundancies as largest positive co-information over reference distributions, and extend the analysis to three or more sources using lattice equations and information diagrams.
result: Hi-Fi and MMI PIDs are shown to sit at opposite ends of the overlap segment for two sources, while for three or more sources zero overlap on all pairs is often unattainable; random distributions show failure rates of 21–100%.
conclusion: The work clarifies structural relationships among PID measures and introduces a new PID based on splitting co-information into pairwise maximum-entropy and third-order connected information components.

title: Combinatorial Limitations Of List-decoding Reed-Solomon Codes
authors: Omar Alrabiah, Rohan Goyal, Venkatesan Guruswami
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For infinitely many rates [MATH], we show that full-length Reed-Solomon codes over fields of low characteristic can contain super-polynomially many codewords in a Hamming ball of radius just exceeding the Johnson radius. Over prime fields, we exhibit full-length Reed-Solomon codes of constant rate [MATH] with polynomially many codewords in a Hamming ball of relative radius bounded strictly below [MATH]. This refutes a recent conjecture that, over prime fields, list sizes below capacity are always bounded by a constant. Together, these results demonstrate that certain restrictions in recent works on explicit Reed-Solomon codes achieving list-decoding capacity, related to the choice of field or evaluation points or to the list-size guarantee, are inherent.
tldr: This paper proves combinatorial limitations on list-decoding of full-length Reed-Solomon codes, showing super-polynomial list sizes just beyond the Johnson radius and polynomial-size lists below capacity over prime fields.
motivation: Recent works constructed explicit Reed-Solomon codes achieving list-decoding capacity under certain restrictions on field choice, evaluation points, and list-size guarantees; the authors aim to show some of these restrictions are unavoidable.
method: Combinatorial analysis of Hamming balls and evaluation-point configurations for full-length Reed-Solomon codes over low-characteristic and prime fields, combined with explicit constructions of codeword-rich balls.
result: For infinitely many rates, super-polynomially many codewords lie in a ball of radius just above the Johnson radius in low characteristic, and over prime fields constant-rate codes admit polynomially large lists at relative radius strictly below capacity, refuting a conjecture that list sizes below capacity are constant.
conclusion: The identified restrictions in recent capacity-achieving Reed-Solomon list-decoding results are inherent, delineating fundamental limits of list decoding for this code family.

title: Functional Converses For Private Matrix-Product Retrieval Under Library-Wide Decoder-Side Correlation
authors: Yousef Nejatbakhsh Malihe Aliasgari
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider private retrieval of the matrix product [MATH] from replicated [MATH]-colluding servers when [MATH], with the innovations mutually independent and independent of the user-held [MATH]. The servers store the full library, correlated with [MATH], which changes both the communication problem and the security definition: a secrecy condition including the stored library cannot hold, as the library itself partly reveals [MATH]. We therefore measure only additional leakage and require index privacy conditioned on [MATH]; both reduce to classical notions under independence. For [MATH] of rank [MATH] we prove, with no structural hypothesis on the map, [MATH], where [MATH] is the replicated [MATH]-colluding private-information-retrieval capacity. The proof rests on a colluding converse for servers storing arbitrary refinements of the demanded messages, whose answers need not be measurable functions of the functional-message library, and a privacy-transfer characterization. Publishing a canonical row-space representative makes the bound achievable for arbitrary independent and identically distributed innovations under a public-setup measure. Under a strengthened observational model (exact correctness, common conditional library support, and full-transcript security), concealment forces [MATH], where [MATH] spans the linear join of all row spaces in the support of the operand distribution; this extends to vanishing error under a simultaneous-decodability assumption. In the full-rank case product recovery reduces to innovation recovery: [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves converse bounds for private retrieval of matrix products from colluding replicated servers when the stored library is correlated with the user's operand.
motivation: Private information retrieval typically assumes independent messages and stored data; this work addresses functional retrieval with library-wide decoder-side correlation, which changes both the communication problem and the privacy definition.
method: It develops information-theoretic converses for colluding servers storing arbitrary refinements of demanded messages, introduces a privacy-transfer characterization, and shows achievability via publishing a canonical row-space representative under public setup.
result: For rank-r operands, the replicated t-colluding private-information-retrieval capacity bounds the functional retrieval rate; under stronger observational and full-transcript security assumptions, concealment forces a linear-algebraic condition, and full-rank product recovery reduces to innovation recovery.
conclusion: The paper extends private retrieval to correlated-library functional settings and provides matching converses and achievability for matrix-product retrieval, but it is classical information theory without a quantum information component.

title: Lossless Source Coding With Marginal Distribution Constraint
authors: Cheuk Ting Li, Jun Chen, Shahab Asoodeh
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider lossless source coding with a marginal distribution constraint on the encoding symbols (SC-MDC). Unlike distribution matching, signal shaping and homophonic coding which require the symbols to be (approximately) i.i.d. following a target distribution, SC-MDC requires each symbol to have a marginal distribution that exactly matches the target distribution, which can be regarded as a perfect perceptual quality constraint on the symbols, and may have applications to wear leveling, source coding with cost and steganography. We give nonasymptotic lower and upper bounds on the optimal encoding length, and exactly characterize the coding rate (or the first-order term of the length) when the source distribution or the target distribution is uniform, or when the source is an i.i.d. sequence.
tldr: The paper studies lossless source coding under an exact marginal distribution constraint on the encoder's output symbols (SC-MDC), deriving nonasymptotic bounds and exact first-order rates in special cases.
motivation: Distribution matching, signal shaping, and homophonic coding only enforce approximately i.i.d. target-distributed symbols, but applications such as wear leveling, cost-constrained source coding, and steganography require the exact marginal to match a target distribution, interpreted as a perfect perceptual-quality constraint.
method: The authors formulate SC-MDC, prove nonasymptotic lower and upper bounds on the optimal encoding length, and specialize to cases where the source or target distribution is uniform or the source is an i.i.d. sequence to obtain exact coding rates.
result: Nonasymptotic bounds on optimal encoding length are established, and the coding rate (first-order term) is exactly characterized for uniform source, uniform target, and i.i.d. source settings.
conclusion: SC-MDC provides a clean information-theoretic framework for exact-marginal-constrained compression with relevance to wear leveling, cost-constrained coding, and steganography, though it remains a purely classical result.

title: A Universal Threshold Theory For Local Properties Of Random Linear Codes
authors: Vinayak M. Kumar, Ray Li, Jonathan Mosheiff, Gilad Shavit
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thresholds for local properties tell us which guarantees to expect from random linear codes (RLCs) and help us carry those guarantees over to structured codes. A monotone property is [MATH]-local if a collection of at most [MATH] codewords can witness its satisfaction or failure, as in list decoding and list recovery. The threshold of [MATH] is the code dimension at which the probability that an RLC in [MATH] satisfies [MATH] crosses [MATH] in a sharp transition. We show that the threshold of a [MATH]-local property [MATH] is within [MATH] dimensions of the expectation threshold. This is the dimension predicted by the best union bound over covers of [MATH]: families of subspaces such that the span of every witness contains at least one member. This gives a general derandomization statement: Any decreasing local property satisfied by RLCs at a given rate holds at a similar rate for pseudorandom ensembles that fool the cover union bound. In addition to previously studied ensembles, these include codes whose parity-check matrix is sampled from a small-bias distribution. Because our threshold characterization applies to all local properties, this derandomization also reaches properties beyond the scope of earlier reductions, including maximum loads in linear hashing for arbitrary input sets, rank-metric list decoding, and list decoding from insertion-deletion errors and burst errors. Our theorem unifies and strengthens prior works on row-symmetric and coordinate-wise linear characterizations, which located the threshold to within [MATH] and [MATH] dimensions, respectively. We obtain [MATH] error for every [MATH]-local property, independently of alphabet size. Under suitable pseudorandomness bounds, the rate loss vanishes for every [MATH], compared to [MATH] for earlier frameworks.
tldr: The paper proves a universal threshold theorem for local properties of random linear codes, showing that the sharp threshold lies within a small number of dimensions of the union-bound expectation threshold, enabling derandomization of such properties for pseudorandom ensembles.
motivation: Thresholds for local properties (list decoding, list recovery) determine which guarantees random linear codes provide and let those guarantees transfer to structured codes, but earlier characterizations located thresholds only up to larger dimension gaps and were limited to specific property families.
method: The authors introduce the notion of a k-local monotone property and its cover-based expectation threshold, then bound the gap between the true threshold and this expectation threshold, yielding a general derandomization statement for ensembles that fool the cover union bound (including small-bias parity-check matrices).
result: The threshold of any k-local property is within O(k) dimensions of the expectation threshold, with O(k) error independent of alphabet size, improving prior O(k log q)-type bounds and giving vanishing rate loss for every k under suitable pseudorandomness; applications include maximum loads in linear hashing, rank-metric list decoding, and insertion-deletion/burst error list decoding.
conclusion: The work unifies and strengthens row-symmetric and coordinate-wise linear threshold characterizations into a single framework that applies to all local properties of random linear codes and extends derandomization beyond earlier reductions.

title: Quantum Noise Engineering In Advanced Ligo
authors: Beg\"um Kabag\"oz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advanced LIGO is a gravitational-wave detector with extreme sensitivity, operating close to the quantum limits of optical measurement. The quantum noise in this system arises from vacuum fluctuations entering the interferometer readout port: phase-like fluctuations produce measurement imprecision, while amplitude-like fluctuations drive radiation-pressure back-action. In this review, we present an intuitive description in terms of complex fields and quadratures, and follow squeezed vacuum from its generation, through its interaction with the filter cavity and propagation through the interferometer, to the readout. We discuss how frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing engineer quantum noise, and how correlations between optical quadratures map onto correlations between measurement imprecision and back-action. We conclude that LIGO is both a gravitational-wave observatory and a kilometre-scale platform for quantum measurement science.
tldr: A pedagogical review of how squeezed vacuum, filter cavities, and frequency-dependent squeezing engineer the quantum noise (imprecision and back-action) of Advanced LIGO.
motivation: Advanced LIGO operates at the quantum limit of optical measurement, so understanding and manipulating vacuum-noise quadratures is essential for improving gravitational-wave sensitivity.
method: The review develops an intuitive quadrature/complex-field description and traces squeezed vacuum from generation through the filter cavity and interferometer to readout, treating imprecision and radiation-pressure back-action as correlated quadratures.
result: It shows how frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing reshape the noise spectral density and how optical quadrature correlations directly map onto imprecision–back-action correlations.
conclusion: LIGO is presented as both a gravitational-wave observatory and a kilometre-scale platform for quantum measurement science.

title: Ground-State Dressing And Delayed Feedback Of A Chiral Giant Atom In Ultrastrong Waveguide Qed
authors: Giuseppe Musolino, Daniele Lamberto, Salvatore Savasta, Federico Roccati
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. At a relative coupling phase \pi/2, the total spectral density is independent of the distance between the coupling points, whereas its directional components are not. Using a variational polaron transformation, we show that the renormalized transition frequency and the total ground-state dressing inherit this independence, while the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral. A sudden switch-off of the coupling releases this cloud as directional radiation. We also derive the spontaneous-emission dynamics in the polaron frame, showing that, after neglecting the local photonic potential, the memory kernel becomes distance independent at the same phase.
tldr: The paper studies a chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a 1D waveguide, analyzing ground-state dressing and delayed feedback via a variational polaron transformation.
motivation: Giant atoms coupled to waveguides provide a platform for nonlocal light-matter interactions and chiral quantum optics, but ultrastrong coupling with spatially separated coupling points remains challenging to characterize.
method: A variational polaron transformation is used to derive the renormalized transition frequency, ground-state dressing, and spontaneous-emission dynamics in the polaron frame, including memory-kernel effects from delayed feedback.
result: At a relative coupling phase of π/2, the total spectral density and total ground-state dressing become independent of the distance between coupling points, while the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral and can be released as directional radiation.
conclusion: The work clarifies how chiral interference and ultrastrong coupling affect giant-atom dressing and feedback, with potential implications for directional photon emission in waveguide QED.

title: Optimal Quantum Metrology With Restricted Controls
authors: Li Sun, Haoze Wang, Chong Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum control can enhance sensing precision, but practical protocols are constrained by probe preparation and the available control resources. Optimizing the sensing protocol within these constraints helps establish what precision is experimentally attainable. We study quantum metrology from a fixed initial probe state under restricted Hamiltonian controls with bounded amplitudes. Building on Pontryagin's maximum principle, we formulate quantum Fisher information maximization at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels subject to a weighted amplitude constraint. The formulation also accommodates stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations. A geometric description of sensitivity accumulation reveals the mechanisms underlying the optimized protocols. Two spin-[MATH] examples demonstrate the resulting enhancement: time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, while optimized waveforms improve upon CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources to improve experimentally attainable precision.
tldr: The paper formulates quantum Fisher information maximization for quantum metrology under bounded Hamiltonian controls using Pontryagin's maximum principle, with spin-based sensing examples.
motivation: Practical quantum sensing is constrained by probe preparation and limited control resources, so it is important to determine the best precision experimentally attainable under these restrictions.
method: The authors use Pontryagin's maximum principle to optimize quantum Fisher information at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels subject to a weighted amplitude constraint, including stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations.
result: Time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, and optimized waveforms improve upon CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise.
conclusion: Optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources can improve experimentally attainable precision and reveals geometric mechanisms of sensitivity accumulation.

title: Field-aligned Measurement Removes The Anisotropy Barrier Of Sample-based Quantum Subspace Solvers For Magnetized-plasma Heat Conduction
authors: Ahn Doyeol (david)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sample-based quantum subspace methods construct a small subspace from measured basis states and solve the target problem classically within it. We study these methods for heat conduction in magnetized plasmas, where the anisotropy [MATH] reaches [MATH] to [MATH]. We prove two results for the energy-norm Galerkin solution. First, if the measurement basis is aligned with the flux surfaces and the subspace contains the poloidal-mode-zero block, the error is bounded by [MATH], where the numerator does not depend on [MATH]. The bound is sharp, so the accuracy improves as the anisotropy grows. Second, in the computational basis, a subspace that misses a single node of a flux surface suppresses the flux-function component there as [MATH], which gives an error floor when the limiting solution is nonzero on that surface. We verify both results on a shaped cross-section and on a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium with ten qubits. At [MATH], the computational basis gives an error of order unity for every shot budget, whereas a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives [MATH]. The same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization. The aligned measurement needs no time evolution, so the circuit is only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform. On a ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis gives a median error of [MATH] with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to [MATH] shots. A trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior.
tldr: The paper studies field-aligned measurement bases for sample-based quantum subspace solvers applied to anisotropic heat conduction in magnetized plasmas.
motivation: Sample-based quantum subspace methods suffer an anisotropy barrier when the measurement basis is not aligned with flux surfaces in strongly magnetized plasma heat conduction.
method: The authors prove error bounds for energy-norm Galerkin solutions and benchmark aligned versus computational-basis measurements on shaped cross-sections and a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium using ten-qubit superconducting and trapped-ion processors.
result: Field-aligned measurement with a poloidal quantum Fourier transform removes the anisotropy barrier, achieving median errors far below computational-basis measurements for the same shot budgets.
conclusion: Aligning the measurement basis with flux surfaces enables accurate sample-based quantum subspace solvers for magnetized-plasma heat conduction without time evolution.

title: Quantum Simulation Of Classical Rcl Circuits Via Complexification And Schr\"odingerization
authors: Huner Fanchiotti, Carlos A. Garc\'ia Canal, Miguel A. Mayosky, Alejandro L. Veiga, Armando P\'erez, Rafael G\'omez-Lurbe, Vicente Vento
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The decomplexification procedure establishes a mathematical equivalence between finite dimensional quantum dynamics and classical dynamics by mapping the complex quantum domain onto the real classical one. Its inverse process, complexification --- which lifts a classical dynamics to an equivalent quantum formulation --- is of great interest, particularly because it enables the quantum simulation of equations that are of classical relevance. In this way, one can prepare the solution of classical differential equations to be implemented using quantum computation tools. In the present work, we recall the decomplexification procedure and also discuss several distinct strategies for performing the complexification of classical equations, so as to obtain the corresponding quantum-equivalent dynamics.
tldr: The paper reviews decomplexification and proposes complexification strategies to map classical RCL circuit dynamics into quantum-equivalent dynamics for quantum simulation.
motivation: The authors aim to enable quantum simulation of classical differential equations by lifting classical circuit dynamics to a quantum formulation, which could allow classical problems to be solved with quantum computational tools.
method: They recall the decomplexification procedure that maps finite-dimensional quantum dynamics to classical dynamics and discuss several strategies for the inverse complexification of classical equations, specifically for RCL circuits.
result: The work presents conceptual and mathematical strategies for obtaining quantum-equivalent dynamics of classical RCL circuits, though no concrete quantum algorithm or performance analysis is emphasized in the abstract.
conclusion: The paper is a methodological discussion of complexification for quantum simulation of classical circuits, but it falls outside the researcher's core interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems.

title: Experimental Demonstration Of Dual-polarization Nonreciprocal Thermal Emission At Moderate Magnetic Fields
authors: Mason Christiansen, Jae S. Hwang, Yi Jie Lin, Aryan Zaveri, Tianjun Li, Daniel Cui, Baolai Liang, Aaswath P. Raman
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which requires emissivity and absorptivity to be equal at each wavelength, angle, and polarization. This in turn places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies as well as heat transfer. This constraint can however be overcome using magneto-optic semiconductors, which break Lorentz reciprocity under an applied magnetic field. However, in most prior experimental demonstrations, nonreciprocity has been restricted to TM polarization, since the electric field of TE-polarized light is parallel to the applied magnetic field. Here, we experimentally demonstrate nonreciprocal absorption in both polarizations at the same wavelengths and angles from a single structure, wherein a germanium Mie-resonant metasurface on a doped InAs layer scatters TE-polarized light into near fields with components perpendicular to the magnetic field, allowing the magneto-optic response of the InAs to act on them. Under a 0.48 T field from a permanent Halbach array, this structure exhibits a difference in absorptivity between [MATH] and [MATH] of 0.035 in both TE and TM polarization at 16.6 [MATH]m. Our approach shows that the magneto-optic response of a planar semiconductor and the resonances of a dielectric metasurface can be designed together, offering a potential route to dual-polarization nonreciprocity at fields available from permanent magnets for emerging energy and heat transfer technologies.
tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal emission from a germanium metasurface on doped InAs at moderate magnetic fields.
motivation: Kirchhoff's law constrains conventional thermal emitters by requiring equal emissivity and absorptivity, limiting radiative energy technologies; magneto-optic semiconductors can break reciprocity but prior demonstrations were mostly TM-polarized.
method: The authors design a germanium Mie-resonant metasurface on doped InAs that scatters TE-polarized light into near fields with components perpendicular to an applied magnetic field, enabling magneto-optic response in both polarizations.
result: Under a 0.48 T permanent-magnet Halbach array, the structure shows an absorptivity difference of 0.035 between opposite magnetic field directions in both TE and TM polarization at 16.6 µm.
conclusion: The work shows that planar semiconductor magneto-optic response and dielectric metasurface resonances can be co-designed for dual-polarization nonreciprocity at permanent-magnet fields, with potential for energy and heat-transfer applications.

title: Amort-v1: Checkpointed Post-Quantum Attestation For Industrial Controllers
authors: Rishabh Das, Gerald Agendia, Jibriel Adjei, Ahmed Oun
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable logic controllers often remain deployed for decades, making post-quantum attestation a long-term requirement. Prior measurements of OpenPLC attestation show that post-quantum signing can consume 88--99% of round-trip latency and that durable state can further limit throughput. We introduce AMORT-V1, a checkpointed attestation protocol that moves public-key signing and durable commitment from individual reports to periodic checkpoints. An ML-KEM epoch establishes per-device evidence keys, devices authenticate reports with MACs, and the controller commits ordered evidence through hash-chained Merkle checkpoints signed with ML-DSA or SLH-DSA. Because shared MACs do not provide transferable proof of device origin, AMORT-V1 adds a device-held disclosure chain whose keys are released after checkpoint commitment. We validate the protocol with a 27-case attack matrix, 149 differential-test vectors, and a seven-node Raspberry Pi 5 testbed with five physical OpenPLC provers. Checkpointing reduces controller cost by 90 times relative to per-report ML-DSA without durable logging and by 878 times when durable logging is required. Transferable device-origin verification costs 2.95micro sec per report, while controller-side scaling to 10,000 identities requires 6.18 micro sec and 155 octets per report. AMORT-V1 also supports rollback-resistant restart through TPM-backed monotonic state without placing durable hardware operations on the per-report path.
tldr: AMORT-V1 is a checkpointed post-quantum attestation protocol for long-lived industrial PLCs that amortizes expensive ML-DSA/SLH-DSA signing and durable logging across periodic hash-chained Merkle checkpoints.
motivation: Programmable logic controllers stay in service for decades, so remote attestation must remain secure against future quantum adversaries, but prior measurements show post-quantum signatures dominate (88-99%) round-trip latency and durable state further throttles throughput.
method: An ML-KEM epoch establishes per-device evidence keys, devices authenticate individual reports with MACs, and the controller commits ordered evidence via hash-chained Merkle checkpoints signed with ML-DSA or SLH-DSA; a device-held disclosure chain with keys released after commitment restores transferable proof of device origin, with TPM-backed monotonic state for rollback-resistant restart.
result: Evaluated with a 27-case attack matrix, 149 differential-test vectors, and a seven-node Raspberry Pi 5 testbed with five OpenPLC provers, checkpointing cuts controller cost ~90x versus per-report ML-DSA (~878x with durable logging), while transferable origin verification costs 2.95 us per report and scaling to 10,000 identities needs 6.18 us and 155 octets per report.
conclusion: Amortizing post-quantum cryptography over checkpoints makes quantum-resistant attestation practical for resource-constrained industrial controllers without placing durable hardware operations on the per-report path.

title: Energy-Time Optimal Decoding Using Expander-Graph Ldpc Codes And Mesh Network Architecture
authors: Christopher Blake
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Within the Thompson VLSI model, the first energy optimal decoding schemes (up to polylogarithmic factors) that also reach clock cycle lower bounds are constructed. Let [MATH] be block length. Then, there is an exponential error scaling function and a binary symmetric channel, such that for all [MATH] that scales to zero more slowly than this, there is a decoding scheme for this channel with error probability that scales as [MATH] that has number of clock cycles [MATH] and energy [MATH]. This matches fundamental lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. The technique uses expander-graph based LDPC codes, a mesh network architecture, and a parallelization technique. The key technical result needed for this is a lemma in graph theory. This lemma is used to show that communication graphs of bounded node degree can be routed through two- and three-dimensional mesh networks without overflowing the memory of any mesh node. Upper bounds are also extended to three dimensions.
tldr: The paper constructs energy- and time-optimal decoding schemes for expander-graph LDPC codes in a VLSI mesh-network architecture.
motivation: It aims to achieve fundamental energy and clock-cycle lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors in the Thompson VLSI model.
method: The approach uses expander-graph-based LDPC codes, a two- or three-dimensional mesh network architecture, and a parallelization technique supported by a graph-routing lemma.
result: For a binary symmetric channel and suitable block lengths, the proposed decoder attains exponentially small error probability with near-optimal clock cycles and energy, matching lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors.
conclusion: The work advances classical coding and VLSI decoding theory but has no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quadratic Extractors
authors: Gautam Chandrasekaran, Jesse Goodman, David Zuckerman
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quadratic source is a random variable [MATH] generated by applying [MATH] quadratics to a hidden uniform string. Previously, the best-known explicit extractor for this model required min-entropy roughly [MATH]. In this paper, we give an explicit construction for min-entropy [MATH]. Even for the special case of [MATH]-local sources, where each bit of [MATH] depends on two hidden uniform bits, achieving an entropy requirement below [MATH] was an important open problem. This is because such sources provably cannot be reduced (in a black-box manner) to our most powerful general-purpose seedless extractor, known as a sumset extractor. Our new extractor bypasses this barrier, providing the first explicit construction to go beyond sumset extraction.
tldr: The paper constructs explicit randomness extractors for quadratic sources, improving the required min-entropy and bypassing sumset-extractor barriers for 2-local sources.
motivation: Quadratic and 2-local sources are natural structured randomness models, but prior explicit extractors required high min-entropy and could not be black-box reduced to sumset extractors.
method: The authors give an explicit extractor construction for quadratic sources and analyze it directly, avoiding black-box reduction to general-purpose sumset extractors.
result: The construction lowers the min-entropy requirement compared with previous work and provides the first explicit extractor beyond sumset extraction for the special case of 2-local sources.
conclusion: This advances classical seedless randomness extraction for structured sources but has no direct quantum-information, thermodynamic, network, or hybrid-systems contribution.

title: Reliability Of Fisher-information Bounds For Dielectric Metalenses: A Site-resolved Rcwa Audit
authors: O. Olmos-Lopez J. Sumaya-Martinez
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We assess the reliability of localization precision predicted for a 1716-nanopillar dielectric metalens using a site-resolved complex RCWA library and a vectorial Poisson Fisher model. An independent calculation reproduces the archived local axial Cramer-Rao bound of 20.7738 nm to within 0.0044 nm, yielding 20.7695 nm under the same ideal detector and 3000 detected signal photons. High-order periodic-cell calculations reveal a 0.1335 rad phase difference at a selected diameter; different substrate-index assumptions prevent attributing this difference solely to modal truncation. Replacing the recalculated coefficients at 39 actual sites changes the bound to 20.7522 nm. Restricted phase-mask benchmarks and pixel-integration checks further distinguish a stable statistical prediction from electromagnetic convergence. We provide a reproducible, model-conditional benchmark, not a physical-device performance claim.
tldr: The paper audits the reliability of Fisher-information-based localization precision bounds for a dielectric metalens using site-resolved RCWA calculations.
motivation: The authors aim to test whether archived Cramér-Rao bounds for a metalens are stable under independent electromagnetic and statistical recalculation, distinguishing statistical prediction from convergence artifacts.
method: They use a complex RCWA library and a vectorial Poisson Fisher model to recompute local axial Cramér-Rao bounds, compare periodic-cell convergence, and replace coefficients at 39 actual sites.
result: The archived bound of 20.7738 nm is reproduced to within 0.0044 nm, and site-resolved replacement changes it to 20.7522 nm; a 0.1335 rad phase difference is found but not solely attributable to modal truncation.
conclusion: The work provides a reproducible, model-conditional benchmark for Fisher-information bounds in metalenses, not a physical-device performance claim.

title: The Lattice Boltzmann Machine
authors: Sauro Succi Hua-Dong Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The lattice Boltzmann (LB) method is widely regarded as a very flexible and efficient solver for a broad class of transport phenomena in fluids, soft matter and related fields. In this paper, we posit that such flexibility is a direct result of its generative nature as a rule-driven information-processing machine. Its update, a relaxation toward a local target followed by a shift along the lattice, belongs to the same class of iterated relaxation dynamics as residual networks and transformers, with the difference that in LB the operators are fixed by conservation and symmetry rather than learned from data. We show that three properties of this update are sufficient to promote the emergence of closed macroscopic laws from the underlying iteration process, the physical content of the target deciding the specific law in question. A machine whose target is drawn at random generates the transport law predicted from its moments. A network given the same three properties on a graph, where there is no lattice, is trained on a traffic process and generates a conservation law of its own. The mechanism has a precise limit, where the damping of the non-conserved modes fails, and on the lattice the macroscopic law gives no warning of it. In this reading, LB is a lattice Boltzmann machine whose informing rules are supplied by physics rather than by training. Its three properties then state what a new ingredient should preserve when it enters an LB model, whether it comes from physics or from data.
tldr: The paper interprets the lattice Boltzmann method as a rule-driven generative information-processing machine analogous to residual networks and transformers, and shows how iterated relaxation dynamics can produce emergent macroscopic conservation laws.
motivation: The authors aim to explain the flexibility and generative nature of lattice Boltzmann methods by framing their update rule as an information-processing mechanism rather than merely a numerical solver.
method: They identify three sufficient properties of the lattice Boltzmann update—relaxation toward a local target followed by a lattice shift—and test the mechanism with random targets and with a graph-based network trained on a traffic process.
result: The analysis shows that the same iterated relaxation structure can generate macroscopic transport laws determined by the target's moments, and it identifies a precise limit where damping of non-conserved modes fails.
conclusion: The work recasts lattice Boltzmann as a physics-informed Boltzmann machine whose rules come from conservation and symmetry rather than training, suggesting design principles for future LB models.

title: A Nonlinear Interface For Phase Transduction
authors: Linshan Sun, Hao Zhang, Cameron Leary, Alex Amador, Sergio Carbajo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Broadband nonlinear frequency conversion mixes multiple input frequencies, complicating the transfer of programmed spectral phase between widely separated spectral bands. Here we identify and experimentally realize a quasi-linear phase-transduction regime enabled by broad phase-matching acceptance and effective localization of the complex frequency-mixing response. This selectivity can arise from coherent interference without narrowing the pump spectrum. We implement this regime through dispersive four-wave mixing in an argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber, transferring spectral phase from 1032-nm near-infrared signals to 344-nm ultraviolet idlers. Transient-grating frequency-resolved optical gating reveals frequency-inverted, phase-conjugating transfer of quadratic dispersion, localized phase steps, and low-frequency sinusoidal modulation. After correction for the modeled pump-induced phase background, the quadratic and step responses exhibit approximately linear point-by-point correlations. With increasing pump chirp, the transferred phase steps become more sharply preserved, and the fitted phase-transfer gains approach unity, consistent with enhanced effective localization. These results demonstrate quasi-linear spectral-phase transduction in a co-propagating broadband nonlinear interaction without spatially separating its spectral components.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a quasi-linear spectral-phase transfer regime in broadband four-wave mixing inside an argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber, mapping near-infrared phase onto ultraviolet idlers.
motivation: Broadband nonlinear frequency conversion usually scrambles programmed spectral phase across widely separated bands, hindering phase-preserving frequency transfer between bands.
method: Dispersive four-wave mixing in an argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber transfers phase from 1032 nm signals to 344 nm idlers, characterized by transient-grating frequency-resolved optical gating with pump-chirp variation.
result: Frequency-inverted, phase-conjugating transfer of quadratic dispersion, localized phase steps, and sinusoidal modulation is observed, with point-by-point linear correlations after background correction and phase-transfer gains approaching unity.
conclusion: Quasi-linear spectral-phase transduction is achievable in a co-propagating broadband nonlinear interaction without spatially separating spectral components, enabling phase-preserving frequency conversion.

title: Percolation Of Discorectangles Oriented Predominantly Along Two Mutually Perpendicular Directions
authors: Yuri Yu. Tarasevich
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The percolation of finite-thickness elongated objects---discorectangles (stadiums)---oriented predominantly along two mutually perpendicular directions is studied, extending recent results for zero-thickness sticks. The angular distribution is the ``Maltese cross'' parametrized by [MATH]. Based on the known analytic expression for the excluded area of a discorectangle pair, the percolation threshold is estimated by the eigenvalue method. The discorectangle connectivity matrix is represented as the stick matrix plus a rank-1 term determined by the constant part of the excluded area, [MATH], which gives the approximate relations [MATH] and [MATH]. Finite thickness shifts the absolute thresholds and affects the first normalization, whereas the second normalization, written through maximum eigenvalues, cancels the additive geometric contribution and preserves only the orientational dependence, explaining the universality of the normalized curves. Monte Carlo simulations of unit-length discorectangles with aspect ratios 8, 16, and 32, various domain sizes, periodic boundary conditions, and union--find scaling analysis confirm the theoretical predictions.
tldr: The paper studies percolation thresholds for finite-thickness elongated rods (discorectangles) with a bimodal 'Maltese cross' orientation distribution using an eigenvalue approximation and Monte Carlo simulations.
motivation: It extends prior percolation results for zero-thickness sticks to finite-thickness elongated objects oriented predominantly along two perpendicular directions.
method: The author uses the excluded-area eigenvalue method, representing the discorectangle connectivity matrix as a stick matrix plus a rank-1 correction, and validates the predictions with union-find Monte Carlo simulations for aspect ratios 8, 16, and 32.
result: Finite thickness shifts absolute thresholds and affects one normalization, while a maximum-eigenvalue normalization cancels the additive geometric contribution and preserves only orientational dependence, explaining the universality of normalized curves.
conclusion: The theoretical estimates and simulation results confirm that the normalized percolation behavior depends mainly on orientational distribution rather than finite thickness in the proposed scaling.

title: Noether's Second Theorem And The Pareto Front Structure In Multi-Criteria Variational Problems
authors: Evgeny Nikulchev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes a rigorous connection between Noether's second theorem and the structure of Pareto fronts in multi-criteria variational problems. We prove that for a family of functionals invariant under a common gauge Lie group, the regular part of the Pareto front is contained in the union of solutions to weighted Euler--Lagrange equations, and that on Pareto-optimal sections, combinations of Noether currents are conserved. Gauge symmetries are shown to impose additional constraints on the Lagrange multipliers via Bianchi-type identities, reducing the dimension of the admissible weight space. Two practical approaches are derived from this result: dimensionality reduction via gauge fixing and scalarization with penalty terms. The theory is validated on three classical problems: the linear-quadratic regulator with two criteria, a model predictive control problem with a minimax criterion, and the double integrator with control constraints. In each case, the Pareto front is shown to satisfy an exact conservation law, and the analytical structure of the front is recovered from the symmetries of the problem. The results demonstrate that gauge functions (null Lagrangians) can restore invariants even when the dynamics break the symmetry, and that control constraints do not destroy the underlying conservation laws but merely restrict the admissible set. The proposed approach yields a Pareto front with minimal deviation from the theoretical curve, outperforming known multi-objective algorithms, and provides a new foundation for the analytical treatment of multi-criteria optimization in nonlinear dynamics and control.
tldr: The paper connects Noether's second theorem to the geometric structure of Pareto fronts in multi-criteria variational problems, showing that gauge symmetries constrain admissible Lagrange multipliers and yield conserved current combinations along Pareto-optimal solutions.
motivation: Multi-objective optimization typically relies on numerical scalarization heuristics with little analytical insight into the shape of the Pareto front; the authors aim to derive its structure from symmetry principles inherited from the calculus of variations.
method: Assuming a family of functionals invariant under a common gauge Lie group, the authors prove the regular part of the Pareto front lies in the union of solutions of weighted Euler–Lagrange equations, derive Bianchi-type identities restricting the weight space, and propose gauge-fixing and penalized scalarization algorithms validated on LQR, MPC minimax, and constrained double-integrator problems.
result: Each test case exhibits an exact conservation law along the Pareto front, gauge null-Lagrangian terms restore invariants even when dynamics break the symmetry, control constraints only restrict the admissible set, and the method achieves smaller deviation from the theoretical front than standard multi-objective algorithms.
conclusion: Noether's second theorem provides an analytical foundation for multi-criteria optimization in nonlinear dynamics and control, enabling dimensionality reduction and improved Pareto front reconstruction.

title: Clifford Bmw Categories And Conformal Embeddings Of Types B C And D
authors: August Bergquist
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we give diagrammatic descriptions of the quantum subgroups coming from conformal embeddings of the form [MATH] for [MATH], as well as the conformal embeddings of the form [MATH], extending the techniques of Edie-Michell and Snyder which applied to conformal embeddings of the form [MATH]. Our main conceptual innovation is the use of fermion condensation to construct a continuous family of planar superalgebras, which we call the Clifford BMW supercategories. The tower of endomorphism algebras, [MATH] is a combination of Birman Wenzl Murakami algebras and Clifford algebras, much in the spirit of the Hecke Clifford algebras. This tower of algebras appears to be new, and already yields some exciting combinatorics.
tldr: The paper introduces Clifford BMW supercategories and uses fermion condensation to give diagrammatic descriptions of quantum subgroups from conformal embeddings of types B, C, and D.
motivation: The work extends diagrammatic techniques previously applied to conformal embeddings of type A, aiming to describe quantum subgroups for other Lie types via planar superalgebras.
method: The author constructs a continuous family of planar superalgebras using fermion condensation, yielding a tower of endomorphism algebras that combines Birman-Wenzl-Murakami algebras with Clifford algebras.
result: This produces new diagrammatic descriptions of quantum subgroups arising from conformal embeddings of the form for types B, C, and D, along with a new tower of algebras with interesting combinatorial structure.
conclusion: The Clifford BMW supercategories provide a unified algebraic framework for these conformal embeddings and open directions in diagrammatic representation theory.

title: Asymptotic-Preserving Tensor Neural Networks For 3d High-Field Kinetic Equations With Applications To Uncertainty Quantification
authors: Tian-Ai Zhang Shi Jin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kinetic equations in the high-field regime describe particle transport dominated by electric-field acceleration and collisional relaxation. These equations are widely used in simulations of plasmas and semiconductor devices. Typical models include the Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck (VPFP) and Boltzmann--Poisson systems. Their high dimensionality and multiscale nature pose two of the major challenges to accurate and efficient numerical solution. To address these challenges, we propose an asymptotic-preserving tensor neural network (APTNN) method. Specifically, to reduce high-dimensional computational costs and memory requirements, we adopt the canonical polyadic (CP) decomposition structure of TNNs to approximate their solutions. We show that the equation residuals retain this decomposition form, allowing high-dimensional loss integrals to be evaluated through combinations of one-dimensional integrals. The resulting computational and storage costs are reduced from exponential to polynomial growth with dimension. To improve the prediction accuracy in the high-field limit, we enhance the baseline AP loss by incorporating the first moment equation. The added loss term directly constrains the limiting flux closure to reduce its approximation error in the high-field regime. The enhanced AP loss can still be evaluated dimension-wise. Numerical results show that APTNN improves prediction accuracy in the high-field regime with significantly reduced computational costs and memory usage. For a 3D3V VPFP problem with multiple random inputs, training takes less than 30 minutes on a single GPU.
tldr: The paper introduces an asymptotic-preserving tensor neural network method for solving high-dimensional kinetic equations in the high-field regime, with uncertainty quantification applications.
motivation: Kinetic equations such as Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck and Boltzmann-Poisson systems are high-dimensional and multiscale, making accurate and efficient numerical solution challenging.
method: The authors use canonical polyadic tensor neural network decomposition to reduce high-dimensional costs and enhance the asymptotic-preserving loss with a first-moment equation constraint for improved high-field accuracy.
result: Numerical experiments show improved high-field prediction accuracy with polynomial rather than exponential scaling in dimension, and a 3D3V VPFP problem with multiple random inputs trains in under 30 minutes on a single GPU.
conclusion: The APTNN approach provides an efficient numerical framework for high-dimensional kinetic equations and uncertainty quantification, though it is unrelated to quantum information theory.

title: A Partial-Matching Proof Of The Neyman--Pearson Lemma
authors: Rami V. Tabri
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Testing seeks to distinguish distributions, whereas matching seeks to identify their common mass. I show that this apparent opposition provides a direct proof of the Neyman--Pearson lemma. Maximal partial matching between the alternative distribution and a scaled null distribution separates them into a common component and two mutually singular residuals. An elementary dual problem then turns this separation into a testing rule: complementary slackness forces rejection on the alternative residual and non-rejection on the scaled-null residual, leaving freedom to randomize at the likelihood-ratio threshold. Thus the optimal test emerges from maximal matching rather than being proposed in advance. The matching profile also determines the optimal power envelope.
tldr: The paper gives a direct proof of the Neyman–Pearson lemma by using maximal partial matching to separate the null and alternative distributions into a common component and mutually singular residuals.
motivation: Hypothesis testing and distribution matching are usually treated as opposing tasks; the author seeks to show that matching can directly yield optimal testing rules.
method: The proof constructs a maximal partial matching between the alternative distribution and a scaled null distribution, then uses a dual problem and complementary slackness to derive rejection regions.
result: The optimal Neyman–Pearson test emerges from the matching structure, with randomization allowed only at the likelihood-ratio threshold, and the matching profile determines the optimal power envelope.
conclusion: Maximal partial matching provides a principled route to the Neyman–Pearson lemma and clarifies the geometry of optimal testing.

title: Discrete History Operators: Exact State-space Realization For Sequence Memory
authors: Bin Zhou, Rong Gao, Zhao-Yan Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A prescribed finite-dimensional analysis of an evolving discrete history need not admit an exact recurrence driven only by its current state and the entering input. We study exact realizations of causal linear discrete history operators (DHOs). Operator factorization and kernel inclusion characterize exact closure, while the cross-projection defect characterizes closure failure for orthonormal analyses. For finite-dimensional history spaces over fixed finite horizons, we distinguish two minimality problems. Reachable task quotients determine the minimum state dimension for preserving prescribed future tasks on reachable histories. Backward invariant envelopes characterize the minimum dimension of exact linear realizations recovering prescribed analyses on full history spaces within the admissible class. The minimum number of additional independent state directions is given by the rank of the propagated closure defect operator restricted to the kernel of the current analysis. For geometrically weighted countable histories, matrix mode transport yields structured exact recurrences and a uniform exponential decay estimate for state transitions. Additional conditions provide uniform Gram bounds and refined decay estimates. A stationary Meixner specialization yields explicit recurrence matrices, an O(N) arithmetic state update, and minimum augmentation dimensions over finite horizons for selected coefficients. Numerical experiments examine recurrence accuracy, state transition bounds, Gram conditions, and minimum realization dimensions.
tldr: The paper develops exact finite-dimensional state-space realizations for causal linear discrete history operators, characterizing closure and minimal augmentation dimensions.
motivation: It addresses when a sequence-memory process can be represented by a recurrence driven only by current state and input, and how large an exact linear realization must be.
method: The authors use operator factorization, kernel inclusion, cross-projection defect operators, reachable task quotients, and backward invariant envelopes to characterize exact closure and minimal realization dimensions.
result: They derive minimal state dimensions for preserving future tasks on reachable histories, minimum augmentation dimensions via the propagated closure defect, and structured exact recurrences for geometrically weighted histories with exponential decay bounds.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical framework for exact state-space realization and minimal augmentation of discrete history operators, with numerical experiments on recurrence accuracy and realization dimensions.

title: Randomly Shifted Lattice Rules For SDEs With Constant Diffusion: Error Bounds Uniform In Time Discretization And Dimension
authors: Du Ouyang, Josef Dick, Ziyang Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study randomly shifted rank-1 lattice rules for computing [MATH], where [MATH] is the terminal state of a stochastic differential equation (SDE) with constant diffusion matrix. Discretizing the SDE by the Euler--Maruyama scheme with [MATH] uniform time steps turns the expectation into an integral whose dimension grows with [MATH] and whose integrand has a nested composition structure; both complicate the lattice rule error analysis. We generate the Brownian path by the Brownian bridge construction and handle the nested structure using the multivariate Fa\`a di Bruno formula and a rooted-tree expansion. Under suitable regularity and growth conditions, we prove that an [MATH]-point randomly shifted lattice rule with a uniformly random generating vector achieves a mean absolute sampling error of [MATH] for every [MATH] and every prime [MATH], with the implied constant independent of [MATH]. To improve stability and control higher error moments, the median lattice estimator is used. The estimator takes the median of [MATH] independent lattice estimates and achieves an [MATH] error of [MATH] for every [MATH]. We further establish error bounds independent of both the state dimension and the Brownian path dimension under an additional summability condition on the columns of the diffusion matrix. Numerical experiments show that median lattice estimators converge faster than Monte Carlo estimators and remain stable as the number of time steps [MATH] grows. For models satisfying the additional summability condition, stability is also observed as the state and Brownian path dimensions increase.
tldr: The paper proves error bounds, uniform in time step count and dimension, for randomly shifted rank-1 lattice rules used to compute expectations of SDE terminal states with constant diffusion.
motivation: Standard Monte Carlo converges slowly (O(N^{-1/2})) for SDE expectations, and lattice-rule quasi-Monte Carlo analysis is complicated by the unbounded, growing dimension induced by time discretization and by the nested composition structure of the integrand.
method: The SDE is discretized with the Euler-Maruyama scheme, the Brownian path is generated via the Brownian bridge construction, and the integrand's nested structure is handled with the multivariate Faa di Bruno formula and a rooted-tree expansion; a median-of-estimates lattice estimator is also analyzed.
result: An N-point randomly shifted lattice rule with uniformly random generating vector attains mean absolute error bounds independent of the number of time steps and, under a column-summability condition on the diffusion matrix, independent of state and path dimension; numerics show the median lattice estimator outperforming Monte Carlo and remaining stable as dimension and time steps grow.
conclusion: Randomly shifted lattice rules with median estimation provide dimension- and time-uniform, stable and efficient numerical integration for SDE expectations with constant diffusion, well beyond the scope of quantum information research.

title: Sequential Certification Of Partially Identified Product Targets: Information Limits And Adaptive Sampling
authors: Abdallah Skiredj, Abderrahman Skiredj, Amal El Fallah Seghrouchni
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the cost of certifying a scalar target driven by a product of centered Bernoulli means when an unobserved terminal gate leaves irreducible uncertainty. Each factor can be queried independently at a price. We derive the exact identified interval and determine when a requested accuracy is feasible. At every fixed strictly feasible interior instance, the optimal high-confidence expected cost is [MATH], where [MATH] is an answer-and-allocation information game; a globally honest procedure attains this benchmark. At product cancellation, we solve the game through a one-dimensional inverse-KL equation and explicit cost weights. For two tickets, quartic projections and rational bounds give checkable global optimality gaps. Joint confidence--precision limits expose a failure of the analyzed fixed pilot: it can cost asymptotically at least twice the optimum. A charged, precision-aware pilot with checkpoint certification restores optimal expected cost in exact arithmetic when [MATH] for effective precision [MATH], including exponential and certain double-exponential precision scales. Pooled rescue preserves validity and cannot increase observation cost on coupled paths. Implemented auditors verify returns by rational inequalities; reproducible experiments show both savings and finite-confidence overhead. These guarantees concern the specified independent-reference model and its scalar target.
tldr: The paper studies the information-theoretic cost of sequentially certifying a scalar target defined by a product of centered Bernoulli means under query costs and irreducible uncertainty.
motivation: It aims to characterize feasibility and optimal high-confidence sampling cost when factors can be queried independently at a price and an unobserved terminal gate induces uncertainty.
method: The authors derive exact identified intervals, formulate an answer-and-allocation information game, solve product-cancellation cases via a one-dimensional inverse-KL equation, and analyze adaptive pilot/checkpoint procedures.
