method: The authors develop two routing approaches: one finding the shortest route that never exceeds a chosen distance without a rest, and another permitting longer rest-free stretches with an added cost expressed as equivalent walking distance, then apply these to Mannheim with a 1,000 m travel budget and 500 m rest limit.
result: In Feudenheim, 99.5% of older residents lived within 500 m of a rest, yet only 33.5% could reach a destination in each of five categories on compliant shortest routes; alternative routing raised this to 61.4%, cost-based longer stretches to 76.2%, versus 89.7% when rest needs were ignored, with median extra costs of 7.3 m equivalent walking distance.
conclusion: The framework helps planners identify seating deficiencies, test improvements, and guide route choices, showing that better-placed seating can reduce rest-related burden without changing street layouts.

title: Efficient Counting Of 2 X 4 Lego Brick Buildings
authors: S{\o}ren Eilers
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We outline the algorithmic advances behind our recent computation of the number 8364925094730088313 of ways to combine eleven 2 x 4 LEGO bricks.
tldr: A combinatorics note describing the algorithmic techniques used to enumerate all ways of combining eleven 2x4 LEGO bricks, yielding a specific large integer count.
motivation: Counting brick assemblies is a hard combinatorial enumeration problem of recreational and algorithmic interest, and prior enumerations were limited to smaller brick counts.
method: Algorithmic advances (likely transfer-matrix / dynamic programming or canonical-form enumeration with symmetry reduction) are outlined to make the enumeration of eleven 2x4 bricks computationally feasible.
result: The total number of distinct ways to combine eleven 2x4 LEGO bricks is reported as 8364925094730088313.
conclusion: The work demonstrates scalable exact combinatorial counting for brick assemblies and provides a benchmark number for future enumeration studies.

title: How To Look Inside The Black Box: A Survey Of Yu. E. Nesterov's Contributions (On The Award Of The 2026 Gauss Prize)
authors: A. V. Gasnikov, A. Yu. Gornov, D. M. Dvinskikh, Yu. V. Dorn, D. I. Kamzolov, Yu. V. Maximov, V. V. Matyukhin, R. F. Hildebrand
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On July 23, 2026, at the opening of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia, the International Mathematical Union announced the award of the Gauss Prize to Yurii Evgenievich Nesterov -- an award for mathematical work with significant applications outside mathematics. This article explains the mathematical content of the recognized work of Yu. E. Nesterov and traces its influence on modern computational practice. The exposition is based on a concept that Yu. E. Nesterov himself regards as one of his main results: the classical complexity theory of convex optimization is oriented toward a black-box oracle, but its pessimistic bounds can be overcome by using a priori information about the internal structure of the objective function. We trace Yu. E. Nesterov's scientific career, then introduce the language of oracle complexity together with a classification of objective function models (geometric, algebraic, and structural), and subsequently discuss his main results in chronological order: the fast gradient method, fast automatic differentiation, the theory of self-concordant barriers and polynomial-time interior-point methods, the [MATH] theorem, the stable dynamics model of traffic flows, the smoothing technique, primal-dual methods, cubic regularization of Newton's method, the modified Gauss--Newton scheme, coordinate descent methods and methods for huge-scale problems, gradient-free methods, universal gradient methods, implementable tensor methods, and "superfast" methods. Each topic is accompanied by historical background, precise statements specifying the problem class, oracle, and type of guarantee, examples, and a discussion of the current state of the art.
tldr: A survey of Yurii Nesterov's contributions to convex optimization, written on the occasion of his 2026 Gauss Prize, covering fast gradient methods, interior-point theory, and tensor/universal methods.
motivation: The authors aim to explain the mathematical content of Nesterov's prize-winning work and trace its influence on modern computational practice, organized around the idea of overcoming black-box oracle complexity bounds using structural a priori information.
method: The survey introduces the language of oracle complexity and a classification of objective-function models (geometric, algebraic, structural), then reviews Nesterov's results chronologically with precise problem-class statements, guarantees, and examples.
result: It provides a unified exposition of the fast gradient method, fast automatic differentiation, self-concordant barriers, polynomial-time interior-point methods, smoothing, cubic regularization of Newton's method, coordinate descent, gradient-free and universal gradient methods, and superfast methods.
conclusion: The article serves as a pedagogical and historical overview positioning Nesterov's structural-information approach as a central paradigm in continuous optimization and its applications.

title: Neyman Orthogonalized Specification Tests For Conditional Tail Index Models
authors: Liuhua Peng, Shuo Li, Xiaojun Song
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop specification tests for parametric conditional tail index models of heavy-tailed distributions. The tests are based on a projected empirical process that removes the first-order effect of estimating the null parameter. Within the conditional Hall class, we identify conditions under which projection also eliminates the leading Pareto approximation bias in the test process, permitting lower thresholds while preserving asymptotically correct size. We establish the validity of the tests via multiplier bootstrap. For log-linear models, bootstrap validity extends to settings in which covariates among observations above a common threshold concentrate and the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix tends to zero. We further propose a data-driven threshold selection rule based on an estimate of the Pareto approximation bias after projection. The rule allows lower thresholds to retain more observations for testing while limiting size distortions, with potential gains in power. The finite sample performance of the tests is examined through simulations and a real data application.
tldr: The paper develops Neyman-orthogonalized specification tests for parametric conditional tail index models of heavy-tailed distributions, using projected empirical processes and multiplier bootstrap.
motivation: Existing specification tests for conditional tail index models are distorted by first-order estimation effects and Pareto approximation bias, which typically forces the use of high thresholds and discards data.
method: The authors construct a projected empirical process that removes the first-order effect of null-parameter estimation, identify conditions under which projection also eliminates the leading Pareto bias, validate the tests via multiplier bootstrap, and propose a data-driven threshold selection rule.
result: The tests achieve asymptotically correct size with lower thresholds, retain bootstrap validity even when covariates concentrate and the information matrix becomes near-singular, and show competitive finite-sample size and power in simulations and a real-data application.
conclusion: Projection-based orthogonalization enables valid, more powerful specification testing for heavy-tailed conditional tail index models at lower thresholds than standard approaches.

title: Randomized And Oracle-Based Feasible Directions Methods For Nonsmooth Nonconvex Constrained Optimization
authors: Nadav Hallak Dan Greenstein
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimizing nonsmooth nonconvex objectives over general convex sets using no derivatives of the objective, together with structural access to the constraint set, poses a fundamental geometric difficulty: at boundary points, the feasible direction cone may fail to be closed, preventing the construction of finite sets of search directions that capture all feasible descent directions. We develop a feasible-directions framework for problems structured as the difference between a continuously differentiable function and a convex function over a closed convex set, and access the objective without knowledge of its decomposition, through exact line searches along feasible segments. To address the geometric obstruction, we introduce [MATH]-feasible directions, which remain uniformly separated from the boundary of the feasible direction cone, enabling finite-direction search even in the presence of nonlinear constraints. We present two algorithmic realizations of this framework. The first assumes access to an [MATH]-direction oracle and extends feasible-directions methods from linear to general convex constraints. The second replaces the oracle by a noise-augmented randomization scheme that constructs spanning directions from the affine-hull inner normal and almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points when initialized outside that set. Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz continuity of the smooth component's gradient, we jointly control the spanning coefficients and feasible step lengths of the oracle construction. This yields finite-time approximate [MATH]-stationarity along every unit feasible direction admitting a prescribed positive step length. For both methods, we also establish a rate in the proximal directional minimization (PDM) measure, assuming uniformly bounded direction-set sizes. Randomized exploration ensures that, almost surely, every accumulation point is [MATH]-stationary.
tldr: The paper develops randomized and oracle-based feasible-direction algorithms for nonsmooth nonconvex constrained optimization with a difference-of-convex-plus-smooth structure, achieving finite-time approximate stationarity guarantees.
motivation: Classical feasible-direction methods break down when the feasible direction cone is not closed at boundary points of general convex sets, so finite sets of search directions cannot capture all feasible descent directions.
method: The authors introduce b-epsilon-feasible directions uniformly separated from the cone boundary and give two algorithmic realizations: one using an epsilon-direction oracle and one using a noise-augmented randomization scheme that almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points.
result: Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz gradient assumptions, the methods attain finite-time approximate stationarity along unit feasible directions with prescribed step length, plus rates in a proximal directional minimization measure, with almost-sure stationarity of accumulation points.
conclusion: The framework extends feasible-direction methods from linear to general convex constraints and provides convergence guarantees for derivative-free nonsmooth nonconvex constrained optimization.

title: Thurston Algorithm For Real Entire Maps: Existence And Uniqueness
authors: Sebastian van Strien
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper deals with the real Thurston pullback algorithm for entire maps with finitely many finite singular values, all real. Given a finite forward-invariant marking containing the singular values and satisfying an interval no-Levy-cycle condition, the pullback is shown to have a unique fixed point and it is shown that every orbit converges to it. The resulting entire map uniquely realises the marked dynamics up to positive affine conjugacy. Thus this paper established Thurston realisation and uniqueness in the setting of real entire maps with a finite postsingular set. As usual, the realisation problem reduces to the existence of a fixed point of the Thurston map [MATH] which in the real setting acts on a simplex [MATH] of dimension [MATH] if the required postsingular set consists of [MATH] points. The key estimate concerns a finite real preimage interval: when its critical multiplicity is bounded and its endpoint values stay separated from the singular values unless they equal to one, its hyperbolic diameter grows at most double-logarithmically as the separation tends to zero. An expansive marking (absence of Levy cycles) then rules out configurations near the boundary of the simplex whose displacement under the Thurston map is at most a fixed multiple of their distance to the boundary. Using a version of the Brouwer fixed point theorem, this immediately implies that the Thurston map [MATH] has a fixed point. The argument permits infinitely many real and non-real critical points and different behaviours as the real variable tends to [MATH] and [MATH]. Additional estimates for fixed labelled inverse branches, which are not strictly necessary for the proof of the Main Theorem, are given in the appendices.
tldr: The paper proves existence and uniqueness of a fixed point for the real Thurston pullback algorithm for real entire maps with finitely many finite real singular values, establishing Thurston realisation in the real setting.
motivation: Thurston's realisation theorem is well understood in the rational-map setting, but the real entire-map case with a finite postsingular set requires new estimates to handle the simplex-valued pullback map and its boundary behaviour.
method: The realisation problem is reduced to finding a fixed point of the Thurston map acting on a finite-dimensional simplex; the key step is a double-logarithmic bound on the hyperbolic diameter of finite real preimage intervals as the separation from singular values tends to zero, combined with a no-Levy-cycle (expansive marking) condition and a Brouwer-type fixed point argument.
result: Under the interval no-Levy-cycle condition, the pullback map has a unique fixed point, every orbit converges to it, and the resulting entire map uniquely realises the marked dynamics up to positive affine conjugacy, even allowing infinitely many critical points.
conclusion: Thurston realisation and uniqueness are established for real entire maps with finite postsingular set, extending the classical theory to a real, non-polynomial setting.

title: Full Provenance On The Coss Causal Axis: An Event-Level Closure Of Causal Attribution And Confused-Deputy Exclusion
authors: Nicola Gallo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) represents an authority-use event as an operation/resource behavior situated in a causal lineage, [MATH]. We make the causal occurrence itself primitive: a represented security-relevant causal graph [MATH] in which each occurrence has a unique causal history, so the consistent event-lineage space is canonically isomorphic to [MATH]. The modeled execution has one causal partial order; distinct lineages are distinct causal histories inside it and may share a root while diverging into incomparable branches. PIC's [MATH] is the authority-behavior projection of this space, and Causally Ordered Security-State (COSS) continuity generalizes it to an arbitrary behavior product over the same causal execution. On this semantics we prove an architecture-independent confused-deputy exclusion theorem. PIC continuation requires [MATH] on every ordinary causal edge, so descendants are bounded by their ancestors; at an ordinary join, authority available on only one incoming branch cannot be resurrected, even when branches share a common root. Non-conservative combination must be an explicit authorized composition or relaxation event. With protected-effect mediation, an effect caused by request [MATH] through an ordinary authority segment can exercise only authority in [MATH], so a confused-deputy state is contradictory. The result holds for any system whose protected request-to-effect causes are faithfully represented and whose ordinary authority transport satisfies PIC. We revisit Rajani, Garg, and Rezk: their value, control-flow, and initial-heap attacks are different witnesses of causal ancestry, so full provenance is an evidence mechanism for recovering edges of the causal graph, not the foundation of the PIC theorem. Finally we lift it to the COSS product of heterogeneous security-state coordinates.
tldr: The paper builds a formal causal-graph semantics for provenance and authority-use events, and uses it to prove an architecture-independent confused-deputy exclusion theorem.
motivation: Classical provenance models (e.g., the Rajani-Garg-Rezk line of work) treat provenance as a derived annotation rather than as the causal structure itself, which muddies security guarantees against confused-deputy attacks.
method: The authors take causal occurrences as primitive, define a space of consistent event lineages canonically isomorphic to a causal graph, define Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) as an authority-behavior projection, and generalize it to a Causally Ordered Security-State (COSS) product over heterogeneous security coordinates.
result: They prove that under PIC on ordinary causal edges and with protected-effect mediation, authority cannot be resurrected at joins along a single branch, so a confused-deputy state is contradictory; they reinterpret prior value/control-flow/initial-heap attacks as witnesses of causal ancestry.
conclusion: Full provenance is best understood as an evidence mechanism for recovering causal-graph edges rather than as the foundation of the authority-continuity theorem itself, and the result lifts to arbitrary COSS behavior products.

title: Spillway: Separating Target Admission From Sanitization To Defend Tool-Using Agents Against Prompt Injection
authors: Woosang Lim (SAINT Machines, KAIST), Yeseul Chang (chung-Ang University), Jaewoo Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.
tldr: SPILLWAY is a runtime defense for tool-using LLM agents that separates target admission from sanitization to block prompt-injection attacks that redirect actions to attacker-controlled targets.
motivation: Agents acting on email, files, and payments are vulnerable to instructions hidden in untrusted content, and existing defenses either put a model on the critical admission decision or require model-driven planning of each task.
method: The system reads action targets from tools' typed returns, admitting a call only when each target value appearing in tool output but not in the user task came from a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule; a deterministic sanitizer strips instruction-like spans before the model reads them, retaining them as evidence, with an optional local judge that can restore refusals but never ones whose target lies in removed text.
result: Across three backbones and seven task suites, no standard templated injection redirected an action to an attacker's target, achieving the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) among the defenses tested, with mean in-scope attack success of 0.007 under a released RL attacker and zero under a forged chat template, at almost no added model calls.
conclusion: Provenance-based deterministic admission checks provide an auditable, backbone-agnostic refusal floor for agent action targets while preserving utility, though the work is entirely in AI security and unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Signed But Not Safe: Requirement Integrity In Multi-Agent Llm Handoffs
authors: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang, Chu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. Signing protects requirements in transit, not at extraction; the extraction step is the trust boundary.
tldr: A preregistered study showing that HMAC-signed requirement manifests reduce unsafe commits in multi-agent LLM handoffs, though the extraction step remains the trust boundary.
motivation: Enterprise LLM agent pipelines split user requests across subagents, and each handoff can silently drop or alter requirements, creating safety and correctness risks.
method: Synthetic exactly-scorable tasks with Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threat classes) comparing free-text, structured JSON, and signed requirement-manifest handoffs, where code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256 and a deterministic verifier checks the merger's decision.
result: Signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0%, defeated in-transit tampering entirely (79% vs 0% violations), and the deterministic verifier outperformed an LLM checker (78.7% vs 59.0% detection, 7% vs 50% false alarms); a pre-signing injection attack raised violations to 37.5-75.0% across models.
conclusion: Cryptographic signing protects requirements in transit but not at extraction; requirement extraction must be treated as the genuine trust boundary in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Transparency In Team Contracts
authors: Paul D\"utting, Yingkai Li, Inbal Talgam-Cohen, Jinzhao Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a contract, sharing part of the project's success among the agents; second, to design a (Bayesian) persuasion scheme, selectively sharing information with the agents. In this work we are interested in the optimal combination of both these tools. We tackle the joint problem through the prism of simplicity vs. optimality, and establish a stark dichotomy: The simple disclosure scheme of full transparency achieves a tight [MATH]-approximation to the optimal combination of information disclosure and team contract, when the team's production function is submodular. In contrast, full transparency can be arbitrarily far from optimal when production is supermodular. The techniques that we develop to bound the gap for submodular functions, also yield a new deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm for pure multi-agent contract design, with a significantly improved approximation ratio of [MATH], and thus a [MATH]-approximation algorithm for the joint information and contracting problem.
tldr: The paper studies the optimal joint design of team contracts and Bayesian information disclosure, showing that full transparency is a tight constant-factor approximation when the production function is submodular but can be arbitrarily bad for supermodular production.
motivation: In contract design the principal usually knows more about project success probabilities than the agents, so combining incentive contracts with strategic information disclosure is practically important, yet the joint optimization of both tools is not well understood.
method: The authors analyze the joint information-disclosure-plus-contracting problem through a simplicity-versus-optimality lens, proving approximation guarantees for the simple full-transparency scheme and deriving new deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithms for multi-agent contract design.
result: They establish a stark dichotomy: full transparency tightly approximates the optimal joint scheme for submodular production functions, but can be arbitrarily far from optimal for supermodular ones; their bounding techniques also yield improved approximation ratios for pure multi-agent contract design.
conclusion: Simple full-transparency disclosure is near-optimal under submodularity, providing both a practical design guideline and improved algorithmic guarantees for joint information and contracting problems.

title: Learning And Steering In Incomplete-Information Games
authors: Tamer Ba\c{s}ar Asr{\i}n Efe Yorulmaz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of [MATH] that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of [MATH], while time-average payments are of [MATH].
tldr: A mediator learns unknown agent utilities from trajectory feedback and steers adaptive agents toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria via a Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm.
motivation: In multi-agent systems a mediator often wants to influence strategic outcomes while not knowing the agents' utilities and receiving only outcome-level feedback, so principled learning-and-steering algorithms with sample-complexity guarantees are needed.
method: Halving-type algorithms estimate utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, combined with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer loop interleaving learning, equilibrium computation, and steering.
result: The learning procedures attain sample complexity matching worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors, and with high probability the combined algorithm achieves sublinear directness and optimality gaps with time-average payments bounded accordingly.
conclusion: Mediator-based steering of adaptive agents toward extensive-form correlated equilibria is achievable from bandit-style feedback with provable efficiency, though the work is purely classical game-theoretic and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: A Gingerbread House For Llm Agents: Source-Planned Honeypots That Lure Autonomous Attackers Into An Isolated Shadow
authors: Seungdeok Roh, Seokjun Ryu, Sohee Park, Daeseon Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents can exploit web vulnerabilities fast enough that patching may come too late. Deception against such agents has mostly lured them away from a real target that stays reachable. We study a different arrangement: an LLM defender plans a static honeypot from the application's source, and a router sends every later request of a client it confirms as an attacker, including a working exploit, to an isolated shadow copy. We compare no defence, this static plan, and an augmented configuration with a runtime LLM responder and further router rules, graded by the benchmark's own grader on the real target and, for ARTEX, also on the shadow. On the 40 critical CVE-Bench tasks the static plan cut real compromise from 26/40 to 5/40 for Claude Opus 4.8 and from 20/40 to 0/40 (31 valid runs) for the ARTEX attack framework. On 20 new tasks not used in the design, ARTEX went from 15/20 to 0/20. In about half of the deception-arm runs ARTEX's exploit succeeded on the shadow while the real target stayed intact: the defence moved a working exploit rather than stopping it, and the remaining risk lies in requests that reach the real target before confirmation. ARTEX reported a planted fake secret as genuine on 30 of the 120 deception-arm tasks, five times in a report that labelled another item a decoy. With ARTEX's real compromise at zero in both deception configurations, they did not differ significantly on the remaining outcomes, a comparison that does not isolate the responder.
tldr: An LLM defender plans static honeypots from application source code, and a router redirects confirmed attackers—including their working exploits—to an isolated shadow copy of the target.
motivation: Autonomous LLM attackers can exploit web vulnerabilities faster than defenders can patch, so the authors explore deception that relocates rather than blocks attacks.
method: The paper compares no defence, a source-planned static honeypot scheme, and an augmented configuration with a runtime LLM responder and extra router rules, graded on real targets and on the shadow copy across CVE-Bench and ARTEX tasks.
result: Static planning reduced real compromise from 26/40 to 5/40 (Claude Opus) and from 20/40 to 0/40 (ARTEX), and from 15/20 to 0/20 on held-out tasks, with exploits succeeding on the shadow copy roughly half the time.
conclusion: The defence relocates working exploits into an isolated shadow instead of neutralising them, leaving residual risk from requests that reach the real target before attacker confirmation.

title: Distributed Optimization Involving Non-Lipschitzian, Linear Composite Functions: Unified Algorithm Design And Convergence Analysis
authors: Liang Ran, Huaqing Li, Lifeng Zheng, Jun Li, Run Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well as globally coupling constraints including affine equality and nonlinear inequality. The terminal goal is to minimize the sum of local non-differentiable convex functions and proximable nonsmooth convex composite terms attached to linear operators, over networked multi-agent systems. This formulated framework not only applies in complex practical problems but also reduces to existing distributed optimization structures. To cope with technical issues caused by local linear mappings, potential multiple nonsmooth functions and coupling nonlinear constraints, we first derive a new local first-order condition, and further present a novel fully distributed optimization algorithm based on variable decompositions and proximal operators. Specifically, the proposed algorithm allows each agent to update states via local information exchange and through {locally fixed step-sizes}, and to find inexact solutions of subproblems without loss of convergence speed. In contrast to existing tailor-made algorithms for the bounded gradients of objective functions or affine constraints, our algorithm is capable of solving more practical cases involving general convex functions and nonlinear constraints. Under mild assumptions, the convergence rate [MATH] in terms of the optimality and successive-difference metrics is achieved, by constructing the equivalent variational inequalities of the proposed algorithm. Finally, numerical experiments on practical application problems illustrate the theoretical results.
tldr: The paper designs a fully distributed algorithm for nonsmooth convex optimization over multi-agent networks with edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints, and global coupling constraints, achieving a sublinear convergence rate.
motivation: Existing distributed optimization algorithms typically require bounded gradients or rely on affine constraints, limiting their applicability to practical problems involving general convex functions, multiple nonsmooth terms, and nonlinear coupling constraints.
method: The authors derive a new local first-order optimality condition and construct a fully distributed primal-dual style algorithm based on variable decomposition and proximal operators, using locally fixed step-sizes and allowing inexact subproblem solutions.
result: Under mild assumptions, the algorithm converges at rate O(1/k) (in terms of optimality and successive-difference metrics), established by reformulating the algorithm as an equivalent variational inequality; numerical experiments on application problems support the theory.
conclusion: The proposed framework generalizes and unifies a range of existing distributed optimization structures and handles non-Lipschitzian composite objectives with nonlinear constraints without sacrificing convergence speed.

title: Regret Bounds For Profit Maximization In Bilateral Trade: Learning The Best Posted-Price Mechanism
authors: Johannes Br\"ustle, Simone Di Gregorio, Federico Fusco, Stefano Leonardi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the perspective of a profit-maximizing broker in a regret minimization framework. At each time step, a new seller and buyer arrive and the broker proposes a trading price to each agent. The trade happens if both agents accept, and the profit of the broker is the difference between the price received from the buyer and the one paid to the seller. At the end of each interaction, the learner only observes whether the trade occurred, and its goal is to achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed pair of prices in hindsight. We start by investigating the adversarial version of the problem, where buyer and seller valuations are generated by an adversary. In this setting, we construct a polynomial-time learning algorithm with a [MATH] regret rate, which is nearly tight even if the valuations are drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions, thus matching the rate for one-sided pricing. Our adversarial algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction. We then consider valuations drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions satisfying the monotone-hazard-rate (MHR) property and provide a learning algorithm with nearly tight [MATH] regret. The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is [MATH]. This last result contrasts with the [MATH] regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.
tldr: This paper studies regret-minimizing learning algorithms for a profit-maximizing broker setting posted prices in bilateral trade, deriving nearly tight regret bounds under adversarial and stochastic (MHR/regular) valuation models.
motivation: Bilateral trade with two-sided private valuations is a canonical mechanism-design problem, but learning optimal posted-price mechanisms with only binary trade-feedback has lacked tight regret guarantees, particularly for two-sided pricing.
method: The authors construct a polynomial-time algorithm combining localized estimation with an information-based minimax construction for the adversarial setting, and a localized-estimation plus stochastic convex bandit routine on the negative log of expected profit for MHR distributions.
result: They obtain nearly tight regret rates for adversarial and MHR settings, and prove a separation showing the minimax rate for regular distributions is worse than the one-sided pricing benchmark.
conclusion: The work closes gaps in the regret theory of two-sided pricing and delineates how distributional assumptions (MHR vs. regular) fundamentally change achievable learning guarantees.

title: Beyond Nine Gates: Classification Of Full-Sided Mahjong Waits With $3n$ Ranks
authors: Xingyu Zhong Shubin Xue
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mahjong is a traditional tile-based game popular in East and Southeast Asia. Combinatorial study of Mahjong hands has been a topic of interest in recreational mathematics, with the Nine Gates hand being a well-known example. This single-suit Mahjong hand [MATH] consists of [MATH] tiles of a single suit ranked [MATH] through [MATH], arranged such that drawing any tile from that suit completes a winning hand of a pair and [MATH] melds, regardless of the tile's rank. Folklore has circulated that Nine Gates is the unique single-suit hand with this [MATH]-sided-wait property. While prior works have verified this uniqueness by exhaustive computer enumeration across different finite configurations, we present a general classification of full-sided waits for Mahjong variants with [MATH] ranks and [MATH] melds. For every [MATH], we report exactly [MATH] full-sided waits, of which Nine Gates is the unique live one. Notably, our proof requires no exhaustive enumeration or any prior knowledge of the classification result. To address the problem in its right generality, a comprehensive combinatorial framework is developed, allowing the number of ranks, the number of melds, and the upper bound on tile multiplicities to vary independently. Reliability of our results is partially supported by a manually curated ongoing formalization in Lean 4.
tldr: The paper classifies full-sided Mahjong waits for single-suit hands with 3n ranks, generalizing the Nine Gates hand.
motivation: Mahjong hand combinatorics is studied in recreational mathematics, and the Nine Gates wait has been claimed unique; the authors seek a general proof beyond exhaustive enumeration.
method: The authors develop a combinatorial framework allowing the number of ranks, number of melds, and tile multiplicity bounds to vary independently, and they partially formalize results in Lean 4.
result: For every n, exactly n full-sided waits are reported, with Nine Gates the unique live one among them.
conclusion: The work provides a general classification of full-sided Mahjong waits without exhaustive enumeration, but it is unrelated to quantum information theory.

title: From What Is Used To What Is Missing: Rethinking Dynamic Rank In LoRA
authors: Peng Xue, Guodong Fan, Guang-Yong Chen, Xing Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA is governed by rank, which controls parameter budget and locally accessible task updates. Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent--normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.
tldr: The paper introduces GEAR, a geometrically motivated dynamic-rank scheme for LoRA fine-tuning that separates tangent-space (within-subspace) optimization from normal-space rank expansion based on a matrix-free normal-spectrum estimate.
motivation: Existing dynamic-rank LoRA methods allocate capacity heuristically and cannot tell whether the current low-rank subspace is under-optimized or fundamentally insufficient for the task.
method: The authors characterize the first-order information boundary of factor gradients, showing the unobservable subspace equals the normal space of the low-rank manifold, then use a local quadratic model to select leading normal singular directions for rank expansion, implemented via matrix-free spectrum estimation and task-induced geometric initialization.
result: GEAR achieves the best average performance across language and vision benchmarks with far fewer trainable parameters, e.g. raising LLaMA3-8B commonsense average from 86.61 to 88.45 while cutting trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.
conclusion: A tangent-normal geometric decomposition of parameter space provides a principled criterion for when and how to grow LoRA rank, outperforming capacity-allocation heuristics.

title: A Bilevel Neurodynamic Approach For Distributed SCAD-Regularized Sparse Least Squares
authors: Juntao Li, Qihang Guo, Deyuan Meng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a bilevel particle swarm optimization (PSO)-neurodynamic method for solving the distributed sparse least-squares problem regularized by the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) penalty to global optimality. The SCAD penalty is nonsmooth and nonconvex, so existing distributed neurodynamic methods have not been extended to it directly. Through two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis, a rigorous full-trajectory convergence theory with explicit convergence rates is established for the inner collaborative multi-agent neurodynamic system without requiring the second-order sufficient condition. A theory-guided inner-outer collaborative optimization framework is further developed, in which a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism is embedded in the outer PSO search to enhance global search while concentrating computational effort on the SCAD shape parameters, thereby improving recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Simulation results on four sparse-recovery scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method accurately recovers the true sparsity pattern and achieves faster convergence and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.
tldr: The paper proposes a bilevel PSO-neurodynamic method for distributed SCAD-regularized sparse least squares with convergence guarantees.
motivation: SCAD regularization is nonsmooth and nonconvex, preventing direct extension of existing distributed neurodynamic methods to sparse least-squares problems.
method: It combines a multi-agent neurodynamic system with two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis and an outer particle swarm optimization search guided by a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism.
result: Simulations on four sparse-recovery scenarios show accurate sparsity recovery, faster convergence, and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.
conclusion: The framework provides a globally convergent bilevel optimization approach for nonconvex SCAD-regularized distributed sparse least squares.

title: Waves: Wearable Active Vibroacoustic Elasticity Sensing For Low-Cost And Non-Invasive Muscle Stiffness Monitoring
authors: Shubham Rohal (university Of California Merced), Dong Yoon Lee (university Of California Merced), Shijia Pan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Muscle stiffness is a physiologically meaningful biomarker associated with a wide range of musculoskeletal and neurological conditions. However, existing muscle stiffness assessment methods, such as shear wave elastography (SWE), manual palpation, and handheld mechanical probes, remain impractical for continuous, everyday monitoring due to bulky hardware, operator dependence, and limited self-use. Meanwhile, wearable muscle-sensing modalities such as Electromyography (EMG) and Mechanomyography (MMG) primarily capture muscle activation rather than passive mechanical properties of tissue at rest, leaving a critical gap in portable monitoring of resting muscle stiffness. In this work, we present WAVES, a wearable system for continuous monitoring of muscle stiffness via active vibroacoustic sensing. WAVES injects controlled vibroacoustic excitation into soft tissue and estimates muscle stiffness by measuring shear-wave propagation velocity through Time-Difference-of-Arrival (TDoA) analysis across spatially distributed wearable sensors. To achieve accurate TDoA estimation with low-cost wearable hardware, we develop a physiology- and quality-guided vibroacoustic sensing framework that effectively screens and refines TDoA for accurate stiffness estimation. We evaluate WAVES through characterization experiments using ballistic jelly and end-to-end on-body evaluation with human participants. Results demonstrate that WAVES can robustly estimate muscle stiffness across multiple users and different superficial muscles while enabling lightweight, wearable deployment for everyday use. WAVES is able to achieve a muscle stiffness estimation error of 13.1% or less across multiple users and multiple muscle groups.
tldr: WAVES is a wearable active vibroacoustic sensing system that estimates resting muscle stiffness by measuring shear-wave time-difference-of-arrival across distributed low-cost sensors.
motivation: Existing muscle stiffness assessment tools (shear wave elastography, palpation, mechanical probes) are bulky and operator-dependent, while wearables like EMG/MMG capture activation rather than passive tissue mechanics, leaving a gap for continuous everyday stiffness monitoring.
method: The system injects controlled vibroacoustic excitation into soft tissue and estimates shear-wave propagation velocity via TDoA analysis, using a physiology- and quality-guided framework to screen and refine TDoA estimates on low-cost wearable hardware.
result: Characterization on ballistic jelly phantoms and on-body human trials show robust stiffness estimation across users and superficial muscle groups, with estimation error of 13.1% or less.
conclusion: WAVES enables lightweight, wearable, non-invasive continuous monitoring of resting muscle stiffness, offering a practical alternative to clinical elastography for everyday use.

title: Polynomial-Time Approximate Efx For Chores Via Flow And Matching
authors: Genjie Qin, Qizhi Fang, Minming Li, Wenjing Liu, Xin Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study approximate EFX allocations of indivisible chores under nonnegative additive costs. Exact EFX allocations need not exist in general. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a complete [MATH]-EFX allocation for any rational [MATH], improving the previous approximation guarantee from a factor depending on the number of agents to a constant. The algorithm extends to EF[MATH]X, achieving a [MATH]-approximation for every integer [MATH]. For instances with relatively few chores, the polynomial-time BRBI algorithm gives stronger guarantees. It finds exact EF[MATH]X allocations when [MATH] and achieves a factor of at most [MATH] when [MATH]. In particular, [MATH] and [MATH] give exact EFX. We further show that the approximation factor \(2+1/k\) is asymptotically tight for our main algorithm. We also construct a four-agent, ten-chore instance in which every complete allocation has EFX approximation factor at least [MATH], improving upon the [MATH] lower bound for submodular costs even under additive costs.
tldr: The paper gives polynomial-time algorithms for approximate EFX allocations of indivisible chores under additive costs, improving the approximation factor to a constant.
motivation: Exact EFX allocations do not always exist for chores, so approximate fairness guarantees are needed with efficient algorithms.
method: The authors use flow and matching techniques to construct complete approximate EFX allocations, extending the approach to EFkX and analyzing the BRBI algorithm for instances with few chores.
result: They obtain a constant-factor EFX approximation for any rational parameter, achieve a 2+1/k approximation for EFkX, and show asymptotic tightness; they also improve a lower bound for additive chores.
conclusion: The work advances fair division theory for chores by providing polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithms and tightness/lower-bound results.

title: Cores Of $3$-distant Convex Games
authors: Keisuke Bando, Toshiyuki Hirai, Kenzo Imamura, Ryuhei Mizutani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. We study the core of [MATH]-distant convex games, which permit violations of convexity only between closely related coalitions. Although the core of such a game may be empty, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition for its nonemptiness. We also develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for finding a core allocation whenever one exists. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the framework to oligopolistic competition with merger synergies and profit allocation of joint production with complementary inputs.
tldr: The paper studies cooperative games that are '3-distant convex' and gives conditions and an algorithm for finding core allocations.
motivation: Convex cooperative games have nonempty cores and efficient core-allocation constructions, but local economic frictions can break convexity, motivating relaxed convexity notions.
method: The authors characterize nonemptiness of the core for 3-distant convex games and develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm to construct a core allocation when one exists.
result: A simple necessary and sufficient condition for core nonemptiness is established, along with a polynomial-time algorithm, and the framework is applied to oligopolistic competition with merger synergies and joint-production profit allocation.
conclusion: The work extends cooperative game theory beyond convexity and provides computationally tractable core existence and allocation results with economic applications.

title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection With Task-Tampering Attacks
authors: Rongting Zhang, Martin Bertran, Sandeep Avula, Chia-Jung Lee, Vanessa Murdock
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent's objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at [URL].
tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark for indirect prompt-injection attacks that tamper with decisions inside an otherwise unchanged tool-use task, rather than redirecting the agent to a new task.
motivation: Existing IPI benchmarks mostly test planted instructions that hijack the agent's objective, so they may overestimate how well defenses generalize to subtler attacks that corrupt the values and rules behind a legitimate task.
method: The authors define attacks by lack of authority over a decision, build 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments where the user names the authoritative source, and craft matched attacks targeting six components of the agent's decision process (objective, decision rules, actions, consequences, observations, state); they then evaluate five LLMs with and without detection-and-removal and tool-policy defenses.
result: Without defenses, attacks on decision rules, available actions, and state succeed more often than objective-targeting attacks; detection-and-removal cuts objective attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation and state attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%, and the tool-policy defense still permits 15.4% success versus 17.0% undefended.
conclusion: Benchmarks that only test task redirection or objective hijacking overstate defense coverage; evaluation should include decision-tampering attacks on non-objective components.

title: First-Order Model Checking On Monadically Dependent Graph Classes
authors: Jan Dreier, Nikolas M\"ahlmann, Szymon Toru\'nczyk
abstract: ArXiv:2611.08143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monadically dependent graph classes are those in which first-order logic cannot encode all graphs. They include all nowhere dense classes and all classes of bounded twin-width. We show that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically dependent graph class. Together with the known hardness result for hereditary classes that are not monadically dependent, this gives a complete characterization of the hereditary graph classes with fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking. This resolves a central open problem in algorithmic model theory. Our proof combines ideas from structural graph theory (graph decompositions), finite model theory (locality of first-order logic), and model theory (counting types). In particular, we show that in monadically dependent classes, tuples of fixed length have only [MATH] types of fixed quantifier rank over any set of parameters [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically dependent graph class, completing a characterization of hereditary classes with tractable FO model checking.
motivation: First-order model checking is a central problem in algorithmic model theory, and the boundary between tractable and intractable hereditary graph classes was a long-standing open question.
method: The authors combine structural graph theory (graph decompositions), finite model theory (locality of first-order logic), and model theory (counting types), showing that in monadically dependent classes, fixed-length tuples admit only polynomially many types of fixed quantifier rank over any parameter set.
result: FO model checking is shown to be FPT on all monadically dependent classes, which together with existing hardness results yields a complete characterization for hereditary classes.
conclusion: The work resolves a central open problem in algorithmic model theory and unifies tractability results across nowhere dense and bounded twin-width classes.

title: Current Frontiers In Mobility And Well-being
authors: Wen-Jing Li, Luo-Luo Jiang, Attila Szolnoki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.07343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human mobility has a profound impact on social structure and collective behavior, which allows individuals to reshape group structures in response to strategy information, acting as a double-edged sword for cooperative behavior. It can both disrupt existing cooperative communities and enable individuals to escape adverse environments and seek high-quality interaction partners. This paper surveys current research progress on the impact of mobility on cooperation within the framework of evolutionary game theory, focusing on specific mechanisms of passive escape, dynamic self-organization driven by active choice, and the core trade-off between migration costs and speed. Mobility, an individual's spatial response to local strategic information that turns location into strategic advantage, influences cooperative evolution by altering interactive information and environmental feedback, consequently affecting sustainable social well-being, such as collective benefits. Under specific conditions, this self-interested behavior at the individual level can foster macrosocial harmony, embodying the unity of individual rationality and collective cooperation. Furthermore, we also discusses inter-layer migration and information routing mechanisms in multilayer networks and extends the perspective to human-machine hybrid systems where mobile agents with information regulation capabilities can serve as information supernodes. Our paper aims to provide a unified framework for understanding mobility as a combined physical and informational driving force in the evolution of cooperation.
tldr: Analysis failed
